sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 frames: IAU 2006 precession, IAU 2000B nutation, IAU 1982 Greenwich sidereal time
@lizard-isana/orb EPV00 model (ERFA, fitted to JPL DE405) for Earth–Sun geometry
provenance.accuracy: Its rotation follows the IAU models listed. The Sun direction was checked against JPL Horizons (DE441) samples; the sample maxima are not a guaranteed bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Body size is the volumetric mean radius (NASA NSSDC fact sheet).

objects.description: Our home planet, with the Moon in its monthly loop about it.

objects.label: Moon

sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 Luna: truncated Meeus-style lunar series, converted to Earth-centred J2000 equatorial
provenance.accuracy: Position checked against JPL Horizons (DE441) samples within the project's acceptance targets, which are not a guaranteed bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Body size is the volumetric mean radius (NASA NSSDC fact sheet).

knownLimitations: The Moon's orientation is the IAU mean-Earth rotation model with its libration terms, so the Moon shows libration in longitude and latitude. It is a published series, not the JPL lunar ephemeris: its sub-Earth point and pole differ from Horizons' by at most 0.01 degrees (about 0.3 km on the surface) at the seven dates from 1969 to 2050 that were checked, and its accuracy elsewhere is not stated by the source.

A landing site placed by the IAU model (a mission reconstruction's, measured at the Sea of Tranquility) sits 0.01 km (under 0.001 degrees) from the same selenographic coordinates on this Moon at touchdown, because the reconstruction and the drawn Moon use the same IAU model (docs/ASTRAEUS_SPIKE_02.md measured 254 km, 8.4 degrees, under the earlier tidal lock).
objects.description: Earth's only natural moon, always turning the same face towards it.

features.name: Eye of the Sahara
features.description: The Richat Structure is a 50 km-wide circular geological formation in the Sahara Desert. Visible from space, it was once thought to be a meteorite impact crater but is now understood to be an eroded geological dome exposing concentric layers of rock over 100 million years old.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 50 km

details.label: Location
details.value: Mauritania, Sahara Desert

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some theorists believe it is the remains of Atlantis.

features.name: Nazca Lines
features.description: Ancient geoglyphs etched into the Nazca Desert depicting animals, plants, and geometric shapes. Created between 500 BCE and 500 CE by removing red pebbles to reveal white ground beneath. Some figures span over 370 metres and are best seen from the air.

details.label: Area
details.value: 450 km²

details.label: Number of Figures
details.value: 800+ lines, 300 geometric shapes, 70 animal figures

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The largest figure is over 370 metres long.

features.name: Magnetic Hill
features.description: A gravity hill near Leh, India, where the surrounding landscape creates an optical illusion making a slight downhill slope appear to be an uphill ascent. Vehicles left in neutral appear to roll 'uphill' against gravity, attracting tourists from around the world.

details.label: Location
details.value: Ladakh, India

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Indian Air Force has reported that aircraft experience unusual magnetic interference in the area.

features.name: Danakil Depression
features.description: One of the hottest, driest, and lowest places on Earth at 125 metres below sea level. Features toxic yellow sulphur springs, lava lakes, and salt formations that resemble an alien landscape. Temperatures regularly exceed 50°C.

details.label: Depth
details.value: 125 m below sea level

details.label: Temperature Record
details.value: Over 50°C / 122°F regularly

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Called 'the cruellest place on Earth' — yet extremophile microbes thrive in its acid pools.

features.name: Chocolate Hills
features.description: Over 1,260 perfectly cone-shaped hills spread across 50 square kilometres in Bohol, Philippines. In the dry season, the grass covering them turns brown, giving them their chocolate appearance. Their exact geological origin remains debated.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Local legend says they were formed from the tears of a giant.

features.name: Salar de Uyuni
features.description: The world's largest salt flat at over 10,000 square kilometres. When covered by a thin layer of water, it becomes the world's largest mirror, perfectly reflecting the sky. Contains 50–70% of the world's known lithium reserves.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: It is so flat that satellites use it to calibrate their altimeters.

features.name: Door to Hell
features.description: The Darvaza gas crater is a 70-metre-wide burning pit in the Karakum Desert that has been continuously burning since 1971. Soviet geologists set it alight expecting it to burn out in weeks — it has burned for over 50 years.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Explorer George Kourounis became the first person to descent to the bottom in 2013.

features.name: Giant's Causeway
features.description: Approximately 40,000 interlocking basalt columns formed by an ancient volcanic fissure eruption 50–60 million years ago. The columns are mostly hexagonal, with some having four, five, seven, or eight sides, and some reaching 12 metres tall.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Legend says the Irish giant Fionn mac Cumhaill built it to fight a Scottish giant.

features.name: Lake Natron
features.description: An extremely alkaline salt lake in Tanzania with a pH up to 12 and temperatures reaching 60°C. Its caustic waters can calcify animals that die in it, preserving them in eerie stone-like forms. The red colour comes from salt-loving microorganisms.

details.label: pH Level
details.value: Up to 12 (extremely alkaline)

details.label: Temperature
details.value: Up to 60°C / 140°F

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Despite its lethality, it is the sole breeding ground for 2.5 million lesser flamingos.

features.name: Blood Falls
features.description: A crimson-coloured outflow of iron-rich brine seeping from Taylor Glacier in Antarctica. The water comes from a subglacial lake sealed beneath the glacier for over 2 million years. The red colour is caused by iron oxidising on contact with air.

details.label: Location
details.value: Taylor Glacier, McMurdo Dry Valleys

details.label: Source Water Age
details.value: ~2 million years

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Microbes living in the brine survive without oxygen or sunlight.

features.name: Fairy Circles
features.description: Millions of mysterious circular bare patches dotting the grasslands of Namibia and Western Australia. Each circle is ringed by taller grass. Scientists have debated for decades whether they are caused by termites, self-organising plant competition, or a combination of both.

details.label: Lifespan
details.value: 30–75 years each

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Local legend says they are footprints of the gods.

features.name: Sailing Stones
features.description: Rocks in Death Valley's Racetrack Playa that move across the flat desert floor, leaving long tracks behind them — without any human or animal intervention. Scientists discovered in 2014 that thin sheets of ice pushed by light winds are responsible.

details.label: Location
details.value: Racetrack Playa, Death Valley, USA

details.label: Max Track Length
details.value: Over 450 m

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some rocks weigh over 300 kg yet still glide across the playa.

features.name: Stonehenge
features.description: A prehistoric stone circle erected in stages from approximately 3000 to 2000 BCE on Salisbury Plain, England. The largest stones weigh 25 tonnes and were transported over 200 km from Wales. Its exact purpose — astronomical observatory, temple, or healing site — remains debated.

details.label: Age
details.value: ~5,000 years

details.label: Heaviest Stone
details.value: ~25 tonnes

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Aligned with the sunrise on the summer and winter solstices.

features.name: Easter Island Moai
features.description: Nearly 900 monolithic human figures carved by the Rapa Nui people between 1250 and 1500 CE. The tallest erected moai is 10 metres high and weighs 82 tonnes. They were moved kilometres from the quarry, likely by 'walking' them using ropes.

details.label: Tallest Erected
details.value: 10 m / 82 tonnes

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Most moai face inland to watch over the villages, not out to sea.

features.name: Xuankong Temple
features.description: The Hanging Temple built into a cliff face 75 metres above the ground near Mount Heng, China. Built in 491 CE, it is the only existing temple combining Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism. Its 40 halls and pavilions are supported by slender wooden pillars.

details.label: Built
details.value: 491 CE

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The crossbeams were inserted into holes chiselled into the cliff face like giant chopsticks.

features.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
features.description: The oldest and largest of the three pyramids on the Giza plateau, built around 2560 BCE as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu. Originally 146 metres tall, it was the tallest man-made structure for over 3,800 years. Consists of roughly 2.3 million limestone blocks.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The four sides are aligned to the cardinal compass points with extraordinary accuracy.

features.name: Petra
features.description: An ancient city carved directly into rose-red sandstone cliffs by the Nabataeans over 2,000 years ago in what is now Jordan. Half-built and half-carved into rock, it was a major trading hub. Its Treasury façade stands 40 metres tall.

details.label: Founded
details.value: ~312 BCE

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Only 15% of the city has been explored by archaeologists.

features.name: Angkor Wat
features.description: The largest religious monument in the world, built in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple and gradually transformed into a Buddhist site. Covering 162 hectares, it is an architectural masterpiece featuring bas-reliefs stretching over 800 metres.

details.label: Area
details.value: 162 hectares

details.label: Built
details.value: Early 12th century CE

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: More stone was used in Angkor Wat than in all the Egyptian pyramids combined.

features.name: Mariana Trench
features.description: The deepest known oceanic trench on Earth, plunging to 10,935 metres at Challenger Deep. Only four crewed descents have reached the bottom. The pressure at the bottom is over 1,000 atmospheres — enough to crush most submarines.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: If you placed Mount Everest at the bottom, its peak would still be over 2 km underwater.

features.name: Spotted Lake
features.description: A saline endorheic lake near Osoyoos, British Columbia. In summer as water evaporates, it leaves behind large polka-dot mineral pools of magnesium sulphate, calcium, and sodium sulphate. Each pool's colour depends on its mineral concentration.

details.label: Location
details.value: Okanagan Valley, British Columbia

details.label: Key Minerals
details.value: Magnesium sulphate, calcium, sodium sulphate

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Syilx First Nation considers it a sacred healing site called Kliluk.

provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Apollo 11 — Tranquility Base
features.description: First crewed lunar landing, July 20, 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin touched down in Mare Tranquillitatis while Michael Collins orbited above. Armstrong's first step made him the first human to walk on another world.

features.name: Apollo 12 — Ocean of Storms
features.description: Second crewed lunar landing, November 1969. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed within 180 metres of the uncrewed Surveyor 3 probe, demonstrating precision navigation. The crew deployed the first ALSEP scientific station.

features.name: Apollo 14 — Fra Mauro
features.description: Third crewed lunar landing, February 1971. Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell explored the Fra Mauro highlands, the site originally targeted by Apollo 13. Shepard famously hit two golf balls across the lunar surface.

features.name: Apollo 15 — Hadley Rille
features.description: Fourth crewed lunar landing, July–August 1971. David Scott and James Irwin explored the spectacular Hadley Rille canyon and the Apennine Mountains. The first mission to use the Lunar Roving Vehicle, covering 28 km of terrain.

features.name: Apollo 16 — Descartes Highlands
features.description: Fifth crewed lunar landing, April 1972. John Young and Charles Duke became the first to land in the lunar highlands. The mission returned 95 kg of samples, overturning theories that the highlands were volcanic in origin.

features.name: Apollo 17 — Taurus-Littrow
features.description: The last crewed lunar landing to date, December 1972. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt — the only professional geologist to walk on the Moon — explored the Taurus-Littrow valley, returning 110 kg of samples.

features.name: Tycho
features.description: One of the most prominent impact craters on the Moon, 85 km wide with terraced walls and a striking central peak complex. Its bright ray system extends thousands of kilometres across the southern hemisphere. Formed roughly 108 million years ago.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tycho is so young and bright that its ray system is visible even without magnification from Earth.

features.name: Copernicus
features.description: Often called the 'Monarch of the Moon,' this striking 93 km wide crater features terraced walls, a central peak group, and a prominent ray system. Formed approximately 800 million years ago, it sits on the boundary of Oceanus Procellarum.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named for Nicolaus Copernicus, whose heliocentric model reshaped astronomy.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Its dramatic terraces and central peaks make Copernicus one of the most textbook examples of a complex impact crater.

features.name: Kepler
features.description: A visually striking 32 km wide crater in Oceanus Procellarum with prominent bright rays extending across the surrounding mare. Its fresh appearance reflects its relative youth at around 1.1 billion years old.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Johannes Kepler, the mathematician who described planetary motion.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Kepler's small size and bright ejecta make it look almost like a splash of paint on the mare around it.

features.name: Aristarchus
features.description: One of the brightest features on the lunar near side at only 40 km wide. Located on the Aristarchus Plateau, a region of unusual coloring suggesting past volcanic activity. The plateau hosts Vallis Schröteri, the Moon's largest sinuous rille.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named for Aristarchus of Samos, an ancient Greek thinker who proposed an early Sun-centered cosmos.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Aristarchus is so reflective that it can look almost luminous near full Moon.

features.name: Plato
features.description: A distinctive 109 km wide walled plain with a very flat, dark basaltic lava floor that contrasts sharply with the surrounding bright highlands. Sits on the northern rim of Mare Imbrium, making it one of the most recognisable features near the poles.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Plato, the Greek philosopher whose academy helped shape Western thought.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Observers often challenge themselves to spot tiny craterlets on Plato's dark floor as a test of telescope quality and seeing.

features.name: Clavius
features.description: One of the largest craters on the lunar near side at 225 km wide, located in the southern highlands. A curved chain of progressively smaller craters arcs across its interior floor. Featured prominently in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named for Christoph Clavius, a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician involved in Gregorian calendar reform.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Clavius became pop-culture famous long before Artemis because it appeared in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

features.name: Theophilus
features.description: A well-preserved 100 km wide impact crater with steep terraced walls and a prominent central mountain group rising 1.4 km above the floor. It overlaps the older Cyrillus crater to its south and sits on the western shore of Mare Nectaris.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Theophilus of Alexandria, an early historical patriarch and scholar.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because it overlaps the older Cyrillus crater, Theophilus is a neat visual example of relative crater dating.

features.name: Schrödinger
features.description: One of the best-preserved large impact basins at 312 km wide, located near the south pole on the far side. Its floor contains volcanic domes and a mare deposit, making it geologically diverse. A high-priority target for future robotic and crewed exploration.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named for Erwin Schrödinger, the physicist known for wave mechanics and the famous cat thought experiment.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Schrödinger is prized by mission planners because it combines impact, volcanic, and polar geology in one basin.

features.name: South Pole-Aitken Basin
features.description: The largest and oldest recognized impact basin on the Moon, stretching roughly 2,500 km across the far southern hemisphere. Its immense scale makes it one of the Solar System's great impact scars and a prime window into deep lunar crust and mantle materials.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named for the two major landmarks its rim spans: the lunar South Pole and Aitken crater.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: South Pole-Aitken is so huge that it behaves more like a geologic province than a single crater, and samples from it may preserve material excavated from deep inside the Moon.

features.name: Tsiolkovskiy
features.description: A spectacular far-side crater with a dark basaltic floor, terraced walls, and a prominent central peak. It is one of the far side's most visually striking landmarks because it combines the appearance of a classic impact crater with mare-like interior flooding.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Konstantin Tsiolkovskiy, a pioneer of astronautics.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tsiolkovskiy looks unusual because its floor was flooded by basalt after the impact, giving it a dark interior more typical of the near-side maria.

features.name: Mare Tranquillitatis
features.description: The Sea of Tranquility, a large dark basaltic plain on the near side and one of the most recognisable features of the Moon. Its smooth surface formed from volcanic lava flows 3.5 to 3.9 billion years ago. Site of the Apollo 11 landing in 1969.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Its Latin name means 'Sea of Tranquility,' part of the Moon's poetic naming tradition for dark basalt plains.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Apollo 11's landing site, Tranquility Base, sits in the southwestern part of this mare.

features.name: Mare Imbrium
features.description: The Sea of Showers, one of the largest impact basins on the Moon at approximately 1,250 km wide. The basin formed from a catastrophic asteroid impact and was later flooded by lava. Its circular outline is visible to the naked eye from Earth.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Imbrium is Latin for 'showers' or 'rainstorms,' reflecting the old tradition of weather-themed mare names.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The gigantic Imbrium impact helped sculpt mountain ranges around its rim, including the Apennines visited by Apollo 15.

features.name: Oceanus Procellarum
features.description: The Ocean of Storms, the largest volcanic plain on the Moon at approximately 2,500 km across — the only feature grand enough to be called an 'oceanus.' Site of the Apollo 12 and Luna 9 landings, and notable for an unusual rectangular border structure suggesting ancient tectonic rifting.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Its Latin name means 'Ocean of Storms,' a dramatic title chosen for the Moon's largest dark plain.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Despite the name, it is not an ocean at all but an immense field of ancient basaltic lava.

features.name: Mare Serenitatis
features.description: The Sea of Serenity, a circular lava plain approximately 700 km wide. Apollo 17 landed on its southeastern edge at Taurus-Littrow in 1972. The basalts here date from 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Serenitatis means 'of Serenity,' continuing the mare tradition of evocative emotional names.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Apollo 17 explored its edge, making this mare part of the final human expedition to the Moon.

features.name: Mare Crisium
features.description: The Sea of Crises, a distinct oval-shaped mare near the eastern limb of the near side. About 556 km wide, it is one of the most easily recognised features from Earth. The Soviet Luna 24 mission returned samples from here in 1976.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Crisium means 'of Crises,' another poetic Latin mare name chosen by early lunar cartographers.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because it sits near the lunar limb, Mare Crisium often looks like a separate dark island on the Moon's eastern edge.

features.name: Mare Orientale
features.description: The Eastern Sea, one of the youngest and best-preserved large impact basins on the Moon. Visible only as a foreshortened ellipse from Earth, its dramatic three-ring bull's-eye structure is stunning from orbit. The innermost ring is about 320 km wide.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Orientale means 'eastern,' even though modern maps place it on the Moon's western limb due to historical naming conventions.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Its ringed structure is so clean that scientists often use Orientale as the prototype for multi-ring impact basins.

features.name: Mare Moscoviense
features.description: One of the rare maria on the lunar far side, Mare Moscoviense is a dark basalt plain filling part of a large far-side impact basin. It helps show how different the far side is from the familiar near side, where basaltic maria are much more common.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Its name means 'Sea of Moscow,' reflecting a historical naming tradition for lunar maria.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The far side has far fewer maria than the near side, which is why Mare Moscoviense stands out so strongly on global maps.

features.name: Lunar North Pole
features.description: The lunar north pole sits in a region where some crater rims receive near-permanent sunlight — ideal for solar power — while crater interiors remain in permanent shadow. Orbital data suggests water ice may be trapped in these permanently shadowed craters.

features.name: Lunar South Pole
features.description: The most scientifically compelling region of the Moon and target of the NASA Artemis programme. The south pole has the largest permanently shadowed areas on the Moon, where water ice is confirmed in multiple craters. Future crewed missions aim to establish a long-term presence here.

features.name: Shackleton Crater
features.description: A 21 km wide crater sitting almost exactly at the lunar south pole. Its rim receives near-continuous sunlight while its interior is permanently shadowed and reaches –173°C. Water ice has been confirmed in its interior by the LCROSS and LRO missions.

features.name: Haworth Crater
features.description: A permanently shadowed crater approximately 51 km wide near the lunar south pole. Significant concentrations of water ice have been detected in its interior. Among the candidate landing zones considered for the Artemis lunar base.

features.name: Nobile Crater
features.description: A 73 km wide crater in the south polar region with large permanently shadowed areas confirmed to contain water ice. Selected as a primary target for NASA's VIPER rover mission, which aimed to map the distribution and concentration of water ice across the crater floor.

features.name: Cabeus Crater
features.description: A permanently shadowed south-pole crater made famous when NASA's LCROSS impact experiment confirmed water ice and volatiles in its dark interior. Cabeus is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that the Moon's polar cold traps preserve useful resources.

details.label: Mission Link
details.value: LCROSS impacted Cabeus in 2009 and detected water in the ejecta plume.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cabeus helped transform lunar polar ice from a strong suspicion into a confirmed exploration resource.

features.name: de Gerlache Crater
features.description: A south-pole crater near several high-interest Artemis planning zones, with nearby sunlit ridges and permanently shadowed terrain in close proximity. That contrast makes the de Gerlache region especially attractive for future surface operations and resource prospecting.

details.label: Exploration Value
details.value: Close pairing of sunlight access and cold-trap terrain

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The de Gerlache area is often discussed because it offers the rare combination of long-duration sunlight nearby and access to permanently shadowed ice-bearing terrain.

objects.label: Jupiter

sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 VSOP87A full series (Bretagnon and Francou 1988), heliocentric ecliptic J2000, converted to Earth-equatorial J2000
provenance.accuracy: Jupiter position was compared with JPL Horizons (DE441) at six dates from 1969 to 2030: at most 1269 km (0.33 arcsec) from Horizons. Sample maxima, not a bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Geometric position about the Sun's centre; no light-time or aberration.

knownLimitations: Jupiter is drawn flat in one colour, without cloud bands: Planetary Explorer's Jupiter map has no recorded source or licence, so no texture is used.
The surface drawn is the 1-bar cloud-top level, not a solid surface.
The rings are drawn as flat bands in Planetary Explorer's colours; their brightness is a look, not a measurement.

families.label: The big four (Galilean moons)
families.description: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto: the four large moons, all discovered in 1610. Each has a Planetary Explorer body package.

families.label: Inner moons (Amalthea group)
families.description: Metis, Adrastea, Amalthea and Thebe: small regular moons inside Io's orbit, on nearly circular orbits close to Jupiter.

families.label: Himalia group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar prograde orbits about 11 to 12 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Ananke group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar retrograde orbits about 20 to 22 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Carme group
families.description: Irregular moons on similar retrograde orbits about 22 to 24 million km out, taken to be pieces of one parent body.

families.label: Pasiphae group
families.description: Irregular moons on retrograde orbits with a wide spread of distances and shapes; Sinope is listed here though it may have been captured separately.

families.label: Carpo group
families.description: Two small prograde irregular moons on orbits further out than the Himalia group (Carpo and S/2018 J 4).

families.label: Loners
families.description: Moons in no published family: Themisto (prograde, the innermost irregular) and Valetudo (prograde, on an orbit that crosses the retrograde moons').

features.name: Pele
features.description: Pele is one of Io's signature active volcanoes, famous for the enormous red-orange deposit surrounding its vent. Its umbrella-shaped sulphur dioxide plume can rise hundreds of kilometres above the surface, while fresh sulphur-rich fallout continually repaints the surrounding plains.

details.label: Plume height
details.value: Up to about 300 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Large red-orange ring deposit near the anti-Jovian hemisphere

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pele's red deposits are made from unstable sulphur compounds, so the colour fades unless new eruptions keep refreshing it.

features.name: Loki Patera
features.description: Loki Patera is Io's most powerful volcanic feature by heat output: a huge, dark, horseshoe-shaped lava lake more than 200 km across. Its surface appears to overturn in waves as a cooling crust founders and exposes fresh molten rock beneath.

details.label: Size
details.value: Roughly 200 km across

details.label: Activity pattern
details.value: Large brightenings have been observed on roughly year-scale cycles

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: At peak activity, Loki can dominate Io's infrared brightness, making it observable from large Earth-based telescopes.

features.name: Prometheus
features.description: Prometheus is one of Io's most reliable plume sources, active in Voyager, Galileo, and later observations. Lava flows interact with sulphur dioxide frost, driving a bright plume that lays down a pale circular deposit around the vent region.

details.label: Plume height
details.value: About 75-100 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright plume deposit around a dark lava flow field

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Prometheus has been active for decades, making it one of the Solar System's longest-monitored active eruptions.

features.name: Tvashtar Paterae
features.description: Tvashtar Paterae sits in Io's high northern latitudes and is known for some of the most dramatic volcanic images ever returned. Galileo saw a glowing curtain of lava here, and New Horizons later caught a towering plume backlit by the Sun.

details.label: Lava curtain
details.value: More than 25 km long in Galileo observations

details.label: Plume height
details.value: About 330 km in New Horizons imagery

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tvashtar's backlit plume looked like a blue-white fountain arcing above Io's limb during the 2007 New Horizons flyby.

features.name: Ra Patera
features.description: Ra Patera is surrounded by sweeping, multi-coloured lava and sulphur flows that radiate outward from the caldera. Changes between Voyager and Galileo images made it a textbook example of how quickly Io's surface can be resurfaced.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Radiating yellow, orange, and brown flow patterns

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The colours around Ra Patera trace different sulphur compounds and temperatures, turning the landscape into a volcanic chemistry map.

features.name: Emakong Patera
features.description: Emakong Patera is bordered by long, bright deposits that contrast strongly with Io's darker volcanic terrain. The light-toned material is interpreted as sulphur dioxide frost or sulphur-rich flows, showing that Io's eruptions are not all the same composition.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright white-yellow flow deposits west of the vent region

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io's surface chemistry is constantly recycled: volcanic gases freeze out, are altered by radiation, then are buried or blasted away by later eruptions.

features.name: Amirani
features.description: Amirani hosts one of the largest active lava flow fields known anywhere, stretching for hundreds of kilometres across Io. Galileo images showed new lava breakouts appearing along the margins, documenting resurfacing almost in real time.

details.label: Flow field
details.value: Hundreds of kilometres long

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io is resurfaced so rapidly that impact craters, common on most solid worlds, are essentially absent.

features.name: Hi'iaka Patera
features.description: Hi'iaka Patera is a dark volcanic center set against bright sulphur dioxide plains. The sharp contrast between dark silicate lava and pale frost makes this region a useful guide to Io's repeated cycle of eruption, fallout, and resurfacing.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark lava patches on brighter yellow-white plains

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dark flows on Io are usually fresh, hot silicate lava; bright areas are often frost or sulphur-rich deposits laid down by plumes.

features.name: Pillan Patera
features.description: Pillan Patera produced one of the largest eruptions directly witnessed by spacecraft. In 1997, Galileo observed a new dark pyroclastic deposit spreading across the surface, evidence of a powerful eruption that dramatically altered Io over months.

details.label: Eruption highlight
details.value: Major 1997 outburst seen by Galileo

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark deposit near Pele's red ring region

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pillan's eruption changed the visible surface so much that it became a natural before-and-after experiment for planetary volcanology.

features.name: Dazhbog Patera
features.description: Dazhbog Patera is a high-latitude volcanic depression in Io's northern hemisphere. It helps show that Io's heat flow is global: major volcanic centers are not confined to the equator, but appear across many latitudes.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Northern dark volcanic center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Io's volcanoes are powered by tidal flexing from Jupiter and orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede, not by leftover formation heat alone.

features.name: Masubi Fluctus
features.description: Masubi Fluctus is a long lava-flow complex associated with repeated plume activity. Its flows and deposits trace how eruptions can migrate across Io's surface, burying older terrain under fresh volcanic material.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Fluctus: a named flow field

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Masubi's changing plume location suggests lava can travel far from its source before interacting with surface frost and launching gas into space.

features.name: Zamama
features.description: Zamama is an active volcanic center marked by a dark flow field and plume deposits. It represents Io's smaller but persistent volcanic systems: less famous than Loki or Pele, yet part of the dense network that keeps the whole moon geologically young.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Dark flow field with nearby pale plume deposits

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Hundreds of volcanic centers are known or suspected on Io, making it the most volcanically active world in the Solar System.

sources: Place names, kinds, descriptions and coordinates: Planetary Explorer's feature lists
Map pictures: USGS Astrogeology and NASA mission mosaics
provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Conamara Chaos
features.description: Conamara Chaos is Europa's showcase example of disrupted ice. Blocks of older crust appear to have broken apart, rotated, drifted, and refrozen in a darker matrix, giving scientists a rare look at how warm ice or shallow liquid water can remodel the surface.

details.label: Approximate extent
details.value: About 800 by 400 km

details.label: Science value
details.value: A key analogue for possible exchange between Europa's surface and ocean-bearing interior

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright rafts embedded in darker, mottled terrain near low northern latitudes

features.name: Murias Chaos
features.description: Murias Chaos, nicknamed the Mitten, is an elevated chaos terrain on Europa's leading hemisphere. Unlike the classic broken-raft look of Conamara Chaos, Murias is often interpreted as the surface expression of a large warm-ice diapir that rose through the shell, breached the surface, and spread material outward.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: About 116 by 77 km

details.label: Nickname
details.value: The Mitten, named for its distinctive outline

details.label: Science value
details.value: A rare example used to test whether some chaos terrain forms by diapiric uplift and cryovolcanic extrusion

features.name: Thera Macula
features.description: Thera Macula is a dark, irregular patch in Europa's southern hemisphere. It is commonly interpreted as young chaos terrain where warm material rose through the ice shell, thinning or breaking the surface and leaving behind a chemically distinct deposit.

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: Often discussed as a candidate place where ocean-derived material may have reached shallow depths

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark southern feature close to Thrace Macula and Cyclades Macula

features.name: Thrace Macula
features.description: Thrace Macula is one of the dark reddish spots that interrupt Europa's bright icy plains. Its colour and texture point to contaminated ice, salts, or hydrated materials concentrated where the crust has been disturbed.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Macula: a dark spot or patch on an icy world

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark patch paired with nearby Thera Macula in the southern hemisphere

features.name: Cyclades Macula
features.description: Cyclades Macula is a named dark patch in Europa's high southern latitudes. It helps show that Europa's surface chemistry and thermal history vary strongly from place to place rather than forming a uniform ice shell.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 107 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: IAU Gazetteer center latitude and west longitude

features.name: Castalia Macula
features.description: Castalia Macula is a broad, dark, young-looking depression on Europa. Studies of this region connect its mottled texture to local resurfacing, collapse, and the movement of warm or briny material within the ice shell.

details.label: Nickname
details.value: Often described as one of Europa's dark spots

details.label: Science value
details.value: Useful for comparing collapse-style terrain with blocky chaos terrain

features.name: Agave Linea
features.description: Agave Linea is a long ridge-and-trough belt formed as Europa's brittle ice cracked under Jupiter-driven tidal stress. Dark material along the fracture likely includes salts or non-ice contaminants brought upward and altered by radiation.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Linea: an elongated bright or dark marking, ridge, or fracture system

details.label: What it records
details.value: Repeated opening, shear, and refreezing in Europa's mobile ice shell

features.name: Argo Linea
features.description: Argo Linea is one of Europa's long, dark lineaments. Its scale and continuity make it a useful guide to the global stress fields that have fractured Europa's surface through time.

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Long dark band crossing brighter icy plains

details.label: Earth analogue
details.value: Some Europan double ridges are compared with refrozen cracks and meltwater features in terrestrial ice sheets

features.name: Belus Linea
features.description: Belus Linea is a dark triple-band feature imaged by Galileo. Bands like this are among Europa's most distinctive landforms: paired margins and a central bright stripe suggest repeated cracking, widening, and infilling by material from below.

details.label: Formation clue
details.value: Diffuse dark margins may record erupted or intruded debris along the crack

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark banding near the anti-Jovian hemisphere

features.name: Cadmus Linea
features.description: Cadmus Linea is part of Europa's dense network of named ridges and bands. Its position among crossing lineae shows how Europa's surface preserves multiple generations of stress, extension, and resurfacing.

details.label: Reading the surface
details.value: Where lineae cross, the younger feature usually cuts across or disrupts the older one

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Low-latitude banding amid brighter icy plains

features.name: Rhadamanthys Linea
features.description: Rhadamanthys Linea is a prominent named fracture system on Europa. It belongs to the world-spanning pattern of ridges and bands that reveal an ice shell continually stressed by orbital resonance with Io and Ganymede.

details.label: Orbital link
details.value: Europa's 2:1 resonance with Io keeps its orbit slightly eccentric, sustaining tidal flexing

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Elongated ridge system west of the central anti-Jovian terrain

features.name: Tyre
features.description: Tyre is a large multi-ring impact structure and one of Europa's clearest examples of a major impact into an icy shell. Its concentric rings are interpreted as the crust's response to impact energy moving through ice over a warmer, weaker layer.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 140 km

details.label: Why craters are rare
details.value: Europa's young surface has been repeatedly resurfaced by tectonic and icy processes

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright circular ring structure in the northern hemisphere

features.name: Pwyll
features.description: Pwyll is Europa's freshest and most visually striking crater. Bright rays of excavated ice stretch far from the impact site, crossing older ridges and plains and making the crater easy to identify on global maps.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 26 km

details.label: Visual cue
details.value: Bright ray system radiating across darker lineated terrain

details.label: Science value
details.value: Fresh ejecta exposes cleaner ice from below Europa's radiation-darkened surface

features.name: Cilix
features.description: Cilix is a small, well-preserved impact crater near Europa's equator. It is especially important for mapping because the longitude of its center defines Europa's longitude system, anchoring the 0-360 degree west-longitude convention used by the global texture.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 15 km in the IAU Gazetteer; NASA topography products describe the impact structure as about 20 km across

details.label: Mapping role
details.value: Defines 182 degrees west longitude on Europa

details.label: Topography
details.value: Galileo stereo imaging shows raised rims, wall slumping, and a central massif on the crater floor

features.name: Manannan
features.description: Manannan is a young impact crater whose ejecta and disturbed surroundings provide a window into Europa's near-surface structure. Like Pwyll, it is valuable because fresh impacts excavate material before radiation can fully alter it.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Simple impact crater with surrounding ejecta

details.label: Science value
details.value: Fresh impact material helps constrain the composition and strength of Europa's upper ice shell

features.name: Tara Regio
features.description: Tara Regio is a geologically complex region that includes reddish, disrupted terrain and lineaments. Spectral studies have linked parts of this area with salts or altered ocean-derived materials concentrated on the trailing hemisphere.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Regio: a broad named region with distinct appearance

details.label: Science value
details.value: Candidate area for studying non-ice materials on Europa's surface

features.name: Powys Regio
features.description: Powys Regio marks a broad province of mottled and lineated terrain. Large regions like this help connect local landforms to Europa-wide resurfacing patterns and to the changing stress field of the rotating ice shell.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Broad southern terrain province cut by many lineae

details.label: Interpretation
details.value: A regional record of older plains being overprinted by younger fractures and bands

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: Europa's north polar terrain receives intense bombardment from particles trapped in Jupiter's magnetosphere. Radiation changes surface ice chemistry, creating oxidants and reddish contaminants that may eventually be cycled downward.

details.label: Environment
details.value: Strong radiation processing from Jupiter's magnetosphere

details.label: Astrobiology link
details.value: Surface oxidants could become chemical energy sources if transported into the ocean

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Europa's south polar region is important because possible water-vapour plumes have been reported there in Hubble observations. If active plumes exist, they could offer a way to sample ocean-related material without landing.

details.label: Observation note
details.value: Plume detections remain challenging and have not been continuously confirmed

details.label: Mission value
details.value: A plume fly-through could sample material sourced from Europa's ice shell or ocean

features.name: Galileo Regio
features.description: Galileo Regio is Ganymede's largest named dark terrain province and one of the oldest recognizable surfaces in the Solar System. Its dense impact record preserves crust that survived before later tectonic extension broke much of Ganymede into younger bright grooved terrain.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 4,439 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 45.00 N, 127.00 W; app longitude: 127.00 W.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Large dark northern region bounded by brighter grooved belts

details.label: Science value
details.value: A reference area for reading the transition from ancient cratered crust to tectonically resurfaced bright terrain.

features.name: Uruk Sulcus
features.description: Uruk Sulcus is a broad band of bright, grooved terrain that crosses older dark crust. Parallel ridges and troughs show where Ganymede's ice shell stretched, fractured, and was resurfaced by cleaner ice or material brought up from below.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 2,200 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 3.40 N, 160.00 W; app longitude: 160.00 W.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright grooved swath near the Galileo-Regio boundary

details.label: Science value
details.value: One of the clearest places to compare Ganymede's extensional tectonics with rift-like deformation on rocky worlds.

features.name: Mashu Sulcus
features.description: Mashu Sulcus is a long northern belt of grooved terrain. It helps show that Ganymede's bright lanes are not isolated scars; they form a global network that replaced or dissected older dark crust over a large fraction of the moon.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 2,960 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 34.00 N, 210.00 W; app longitude: 150.00 E.

details.label: Map cue

features.name: Harpagia Sulcus
features.description: Harpagia Sulcus is a southern grooved lane that illustrates the same extensional style seen across Ganymede's bright terrain. Its position away from Galileo Regio helps make the point that tectonic resurfacing was global rather than confined to one famous hemisphere.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 1,400 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 11.80 S, 313.50 W; app longitude: 46.50 E.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Southern bright-groove system crossing darker background terrain

features.name: Gilgamesh
features.description: Gilgamesh is the named crater at the center of a much broader relaxed impact complex in Ganymede's southern hemisphere. The surrounding subdued rings and softened topography show how warm ice can slowly flow after an impact and blur what began as sharp relief.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 153 km for the named crater

details.label: Broader context
details.value: The surrounding multi-ring Gilgamesh impact complex is commonly described at several hundred kilometres across.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 62.84 S, 124.83 W; app longitude: 124.83 W.

details.label: Science value
details.value: A strong example of viscous relaxation in an icy crust.

features.name: Osiris
features.description: Osiris is a bright ray crater used here as a visual anchor for fresher ice exposures on Ganymede. Its pale ejecta rays stand out because impact excavation exposed cleaner ice that has not yet been fully darkened by space weathering.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright ray pattern in southern mid-latitudes

details.label: Science value
details.value: Fresh ray craters provide a contrast against Ganymede's old dark terrain and help reveal the brightness of excavated ice.

features.name: Tros
features.description: Tros is an ancient crater whose outline is partly softened by the slow flow of ice. It is useful for explaining palimpsests: impact scars that remain readable even after their topography has been muted by viscous relaxation.

features.name: Nanshe Catena
features.description: Nanshe Catena is a short chain of aligned craters in Ganymede's low northern latitudes. Catenae like this are useful evidence for clustered impacts, including debris that arrived in a string rather than as a single isolated body.

features.name: Enki Catena

features.name: Buto Facula

features.name: Coptos Facula

details.value: Large low-latitude facula near other bright palimpsest targets

features.name: Lakhmu Fossae
features.description: Lakhmu Fossae is an enormous system of long narrow depressions and furrows crossing much of Ganymede's northern terrain. Its scale connects local grooves and troughs to the broader tectonic architecture of the ice shell.

details.value: Large northern fossa system spanning a wide longitude range

features.name: Zu Fossae
features.description: Zu Fossae is a broad northern system of troughs and furrows associated with Ganymede's tectonic and impact-modified crust. Together with Lakhmu Fossae, it helps show that Ganymede's dark terrain preserves large structural patterns as well as craters.

features.name: Anshar Sulcus
features.description: Anshar Sulcus is a grooved terrain lane that has been studied as a key example of Ganymede's tectonic resurfacing. Its ridges, troughs, and local cross-cutting structures help explain how bright terrain was built by extension and shear in the icy shell.

details.value: About 1,372 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 18.90 N, 198.70 W; app longitude: 161.30 E.

details.value: A good target for discussing groove formation and strike-slip deformation on Ganymede.

features.name: Dardanus Sulcus
features.description: Dardanus Sulcus is a southern grooved terrain belt. It extends the sulci set into Ganymede's southern hemisphere and helps compare resurfaced bright lanes with nearby darker cratered provinces.

features.name: Mysia Sulci
features.description: Mysia Sulci is one of Ganymede's largest named sulci systems, stretching across thousands of kilometres. Its scale makes it a useful capstone feature for explaining that Ganymede's grooved terrain is a global resurfacing network rather than a set of local cracks.

features.name: Nicholson Regio
features.description: Nicholson Regio is a southern dark-terrain province that preserves ancient, densely cratered crust. It broadens the tour beyond Galileo Regio and helps compare old dark terrain on different hemispheres of Ganymede.

details.label: Science value

features.name: Barnard Regio
features.description: Barnard Regio is a major dark terrain province straddling Ganymede's low southern latitudes. Its broad, cratered surface helps frame the scale of Ganymede's older crustal blocks before the moon's bright grooved lanes cut across them.

details.value: About 3,200 km

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Large dark province near the prime-meridian side of the texture

features.name: Marius Regio
features.description: Marius Regio is one of Ganymede's largest named dark terrain regions. It sits beside bright grooved belts, making it a strong teaching target for how younger tectonic terrain fragmented older cratered crust.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 4,940 km

details.label: Coordinate source

details.value: Broad low-latitude dark terrain near the Uruk and Mashu grooved systems

features.name: Melotte Regio
features.description: Melotte Regio is a large named region on Ganymede's trailing-side terrain. Including it gives the fact sheet a wider longitudinal spread and helps students compare several dark provinces rather than treating Galileo Regio as the whole story.

features.name: North Polar Cap
features.description: Ganymede's north polar region is brightened by water frost and shaped by charged particles moving through Jupiter's magnetosphere. Because Ganymede has its own internally generated magnetic field, its poles are also tied to auroral activity and plasma interactions unlike any other moon.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright high-latitude cap; longitude is a representative anchor rather than a named IAU feature center

details.label: Science value
details.value: Connects surface frost, Jupiter's plasma environment, and Ganymede's unique intrinsic magnetic field.

features.name: South Polar Cap
features.description: Ganymede's south polar region mirrors the northern frost story, with bright water-ice deposits concentrated at high latitude. Future close orbital observations by ESA's JUICE mission should sharpen how the polar caps connect to surface composition, magnetic-field geometry, and plasma weathering.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright high southern cap; longitude is a representative anchor rather than a named IAU feature center

details.label: Science value
details.value: A natural endpoint for explaining why Ganymede is both an icy world and a magnetized world.

features.name: Valhalla
features.description: Valhalla is Callisto's signature landmark and one of the Solar System's largest known impact structures. A bright central zone is surrounded by an enormous pattern of concentric fractures where Callisto's cold, icy crust rang outward after an ancient collision.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 3,000 km for the named ringed feature

details.label: Central bright zone
details.value: Roughly 600 km across in Galileo-era imaging

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright bullseye-like terrain near 15-17 degrees north, about 122-124 degrees east in the app view

details.label: Science value
details.value: The rings show how impact energy spread through a rigid ice shell without the global resurfacing seen on Europa or Ganymede.

features.name: Asgard
features.description: Asgard is Callisto's second-largest named multi-ring basin. Its broad pale interior and surrounding arcs sit in the northern hemisphere, preserving a second example of the way major impacts fractured Callisto's ice-rich crust.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 1,400 km

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Large pale ringed terrain near 32 degrees north, 40 degrees east in the app view

details.value: Asgard helps compare different generations of basin formation on a world with very little later geologic erasure.

features.name: Adlinda
features.description: Adlinda is a large southern multi-ring basin, smaller than Valhalla and Asgard but still vast on a moon only about 4,821 km wide. Its subdued arcs and degraded terrain show how ancient impacts can remain readable even after billions of years of micrometeorite gardening and slow ice relaxation.

details.label: IAU diameter
details.value: About 840 km

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Southern hemisphere ringed terrain near 49 degrees south, 144 degrees east in the app view

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: Adlinda extends the basin story away from the bright Valhalla hemisphere and helps show that giant impacts scarred Callisto globally.

features.name: Utgard
features.description: Utgard is a large ringed feature near Asgard, making the region one of Callisto's richest impact-basin neighborhoods. Its overlap with older and younger markings gives the surface a layered, palimpsest-like appearance.

details.label: Map cue

features.name: Kol Facula

features.name: Lofn

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: Callisto's north polar region is a densely cratered ancient landscape that has remained largely geologically quiet for billions of years. Unlike Io, Europa, and Ganymede, Callisto is not locked in the same strong orbital resonance, so Jupiter's tides have not continually refreshed its surface.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: High northern cratered terrain above 80 degrees north

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: The polar regions help show that Callisto's old impact record is global, not limited to the famous basin hemisphere.

details.label: Exploration note
details.value: Callisto's distance from Jupiter keeps it outside the most intense radiation zones around the planet.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Callisto's south polar region continues the moon's ancient cratered character into high southern latitudes. Its terrain is a reminder that Callisto is a fossilized record of early outer Solar System bombardment, with far less resurfacing than the inner Galilean moons.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: High southern cratered terrain below 80 degrees south

details.label: Exploration note
details.value: Callisto has been discussed as a potential future staging point because it offers solid terrain with a much lower radiation burden than Io or Europa.

details.label: Science value
details.value: Comparing both poles with Valhalla and Asgard helps separate global crater saturation from local basin structure.

panels.title: The most volcanic world we know
body: Io is only a little bigger than our Moon, yet it has hundreds of volcanoes, more than anywhere else in the solar system. Some throw fountains of lava high above the ground.
In late 1999 the Galileo spacecraft flew past Io and caught one of those fountains erupting.
details: NASA: Io is "the most volcanically active world in the solar system", with hundreds of volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of kilometres high.
Io's mean radius is 1,821.5 km; the Moon's is 1,737.4 km (NASA fact sheets).
Galileo, in orbit around Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, caught an eruption at Tvashtar Catena on 25 November 1999, with lava fountains up to 1.5 km above the surface (NASA Photojournal PIA02545).
The scene draws Io where NASA JPL's Horizons system places it; it shows no volcanoes or eruptions. This moment is chosen near the start of the scene so the first panel opens soon after play.
sources: NASA Science, Io: "the most volcanically active world in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of miles (or kilometers) high"; "only slightly larger than Earth's Moon"; https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-moons/io/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

panels.title: Squeezed by a giant
body: Io's path around Jupiter is not quite a circle, so the giant planet's pull on it keeps changing. Io is squeezed and relaxed again and again, like a stress ball in a restless hand, and the squeezing heats it from inside.
Scientists worked this out in 1979 and predicted volcanoes, just days before the Voyager 1 spacecraft saw them erupting.
details: Io's orbital eccentricity is about 0.004 (NASA fact sheet). NASA describes Io as "caught in a tug-of-war" between Jupiter's gravity and the smaller, precisely timed pulls of Europa and Ganymede, which keep its orbit from becoming circular.

Peale, Cassen and Reynolds published the prediction in Science on 2 March 1979. Voyager 1 passed Io three days later, and navigation engineer Linda Morabito found the first volcanic plume in its images four days after the encounter (Morabito 2012).
Tidal heating is the accepted model of what powers Io's volcanoes, hence the modelled badge. The stress-ball comparison is a picture, not a measurement.
This moment is chosen for pacing; nothing special happens at this time.
sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Jovian Satellite Fact Sheet: Io eccentricity 0.004, orbital period 1.769138 days; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/joviansatfact.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Science, Io: "caught in a tug-of-war between Jupiter's massive gravity and the smaller but precisely timed pulls" of Europa and Ganymede; https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-moons/io/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

Morabito, L. A. 2012, Discovery of Volcanic Activity on Io: A Historical Review, arXiv 1211.2554

panels.title: Four laps, two laps, one lap
body: Io has two big neighbours farther out, Europa and Ganymede. In about a week, Io circles Jupiter four times, Europa twice and Ganymede once, and then the pattern repeats.
This steady beat keeps tugging Io's path out of round, so the squeezing never stops. You can watch Europa and Ganymede keep the beat in this scene.
details: Orbital periods: Io 1.769 days (about 42.5 hours), Europa 3.551 days, Ganymede 7.155 days (NASA fact sheet). Four Io orbits take 7.08 days and two Europa orbits 7.10 days.
This moment is seven days after the scene starts: in that week Io has gone round Jupiter about four times. The moons' positions in this scene come from NASA JPL's Horizons system.

features.name: Olympus Mons
features.description: The tallest known volcano in the Solar System, rising about 22 km above the surrounding plains and spanning roughly 600 km across. Its broad shield shape formed from countless low-viscosity lava flows over a very long period of Martian geological history.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: If Olympus Mons stood on Earth, its summit would rise far above the altitude where most passenger aircraft cruise.

features.name: Arsia Mons
features.description: The southernmost of the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes, known for its huge caldera and long apron of lava flows. Clouds often form over Arsia Mons during the Martian morning, making it one of the most visually dynamic volcanoes on the planet.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Arsia Mons regularly grows a giant elongated cloud at dawn, one of the most distinctive recurring weather features on Mars.

features.name: Pavonis Mons
features.description: The central volcano of the Tharsis Montes chain, rising nearly 14 km above the surrounding terrain. Its slopes preserve lava-flow textures and skylight pits that hint at lava tubes beneath the surface.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Possible lava-tube skylights around Pavonis Mons make it a favorite candidate in discussions about future human shelters on Mars.

features.name: Ascraeus Mons
features.description: The northernmost of the Tharsis Montes volcanoes, with a summit caldera complex and extensive lava plains around its flanks. Like the other giant shield volcanoes, it records a long volcanic history on a planet without active plate tectonics.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Mars lacks moving tectonic plates, giant volcanoes like Ascraeus Mons could keep stacking eruptions in one place for immense spans of time.

features.name: Elysium Mons
features.description: The largest volcano in the Elysium region and one of the youngest major volcanic provinces on Mars. Its smoother flanks and surrounding lava plains suggest volcanic activity persisted here later than in many other parts of the planet.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Elysium Mons belongs to a volcanic province that may have remained active much later than the classic Tharsis giants.

features.name: Valles Marineris
features.description: A colossal canyon system stretching over 4,000 km across Mars, up to 200 km wide and 7 km deep in places. It likely formed from crustal stretching associated with the rise of the Tharsis region, then widened through landslides and erosion.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Valles Marineris is so vast that if laid across Earth it would stretch roughly coast to coast across the United States.

features.name: Noctis Labyrinthus
features.description: A maze of steep-walled valleys and collapsed blocks at the western end of Valles Marineris. The region looks like a broken crustal puzzle, preserving evidence of extension and collapse as Tharsis rose nearby.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Its name means 'Labyrinth of the Night,' which is fitting because the terrain looks like giant stone corridors shattered into a maze.

features.name: Candor Chasma
features.description: One of the major troughs within Valles Marineris, famous for layered deposits that may record ancient lakes, ash falls, or long-term sedimentation. Its exposed strata make it one of the best places to study the environmental history of Mars.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Candor Chasma's stacked layers are so striking that scientists still debate whether they formed from water, volcanic ash, or both.

features.name: Hebes Chasma
features.description: An enclosed canyon north of the main Valles Marineris troughs, containing a massive central mound of layered material. Its unusual enclosed form and dramatic stratigraphy have made it a long-standing target for geological interpretation.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Hebes Chasma is unusual because it is largely enclosed, like a giant boxed-in canyon with a layered mountain rising from inside it.

features.name: Hellas Planitia
features.description: A giant impact basin over 2,000 km across and one of the deepest topographic depressions on Mars. Its low elevation allows the atmosphere here to become denser than average, and seasonal frosts and dust activity often gather within the basin.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Air pressure in Hellas Planitia can be significantly higher than average for Mars simply because the basin floor sits so deep.

features.name: Isidis Planitia
features.description: A broad impact basin on the boundary between the ancient highlands and younger northern plains. Its geological setting helps scientists study the transition between very different eras of Martian crustal history.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Isidis Planitia sits right on one of Mars' biggest geologic boundaries, where the battered old south meets the smoother north.

features.name: Utopia Planitia
features.description: The largest recognized impact basin on Mars, now buried beneath the northern plains. Radar and geomorphology suggest this region may preserve water-ice-rich ground and sedimentary records from the planet's climatic past.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Utopia Planitia hosted China's Zhurong rover, making it part of the first successful Chinese surface mission to Mars.

features.name: Jezero Crater
features.description: An ancient crater once occupied by a lake, with a beautifully preserved river delta feeding into its western side. Jezero was selected for the Perseverance rover because it offers one of the best places on Mars to search for signs of ancient microbial life.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Jezero means 'lake' in several Slavic languages, a fitting name for a crater that once held one.

features.name: Gale Crater
features.description: A 154 km wide crater containing Mount Sharp, a towering layered mound that preserves a long environmental record. Curiosity landed here in 2012 and has spent years climbing the mound to read Mars' climate history layer by layer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Curiosity's landing ellipse inside Gale was so complex that NASA used a guided entry system and sky crane to pull it off.

features.name: Viking 1 Landing Site
features.description: The site where Viking 1 became the first successful spacecraft to land and operate on Mars in 1976. It returned panoramic images, weather measurements, and the first in situ biological experiments performed on Martian soil.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Viking 1 kept operating for years after landing, dramatically outliving its original planned mission.

features.name: Mars Pathfinder
features.description: Mars Pathfinder landed in Ares Vallis in 1997 and deployed Sojourner, the first rover to operate on another planet. The mission demonstrated lower-cost surface exploration and reignited global enthusiasm for Mars exploration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Sojourner was only microwave-oven sized, but it proved that rovers could work on Mars and changed mission design for decades.

features.name: Spirit at Gusev Crater
features.description: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater in 2004 to explore what was once thought to be an ancient lake basin. The rover instead found volcanic rocks at first, then later uncovered strong evidence of past hydrothermal activity in the Columbia Hills.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Spirit eventually got stuck in soft soil and became a stationary science platform before Mars winter finally silenced it.

features.name: Opportunity at Meridiani Planum
features.description: Opportunity landed in 2004 and operated for nearly 15 years, far beyond its original mission. It found convincing evidence that liquid water once altered rocks and soils across Meridiani Planum.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Opportunity drove a marathon's distance on Mars, far beyond what its designers expected from a 90-sol mission.

features.name: Curiosity at Bradbury Landing
features.description: Curiosity touched down inside Gale Crater in 2012 using the dramatic sky crane system. Its mission established that ancient Mars once hosted habitable environments with persistent liquid water and the chemical ingredients needed for life.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Curiosity carries a laser instrument that can zap distant rocks and read their chemistry from the resulting plasma flash.

features.name: Perseverance at Jezero Crater
features.description: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater in 2021 to cache rock samples for a future return to Earth. It is exploring an ancient delta environment while testing new technologies, including the Ingenuity helicopter demonstration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Perseverance brought Ingenuity, the tiny helicopter that achieved the first powered flights on another world.

features.name: Planum Boreum
features.description: The broad layered northern polar cap of Mars, built from water ice and dust deposited over many climate cycles. Its internal layers are a frozen archive of changes in Martian tilt, atmosphere, and seasonal transport.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The layered ice and dust here act a bit like tree rings, preserving a long climate history of the planet.

features.name: Planum Australe
features.description: The southern polar region of Mars, marked by layered deposits and a seasonal blanket of carbon dioxide frost. It preserves evidence of long-term climate cycling and contains some of the planet's most extreme seasonal changes.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Each winter, dry-ice frost spreads across the south polar region and then partly sublimates away when sunlight returns.

features.name: Alba Mons
features.description: A vast low-relief volcano north of the main Tharsis giants, with lava flows and fractures spread across an enormous footprint. Alba Mons is less dramatic in height than Olympus Mons, but its sheer width makes it one of the broadest volcanic constructs on Mars.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Alba Mons is so broad and gently sloped that it would feel more like crossing a raised continent than climbing a steep mountain.

features.name: Hecates Tholus
features.description: A large volcanic mountain in the Elysium region marked by summit collapse features and flanks cut by channels and valleys. It helps show that Martian volcanism was not limited to the most famous giant shields.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Unlike the immense shield volcanoes, Hecates Tholus preserves signs of both volcanic construction and later erosion on its slopes.

features.name: Ius Chasma
features.description: A major western trough of Valles Marineris with steep walls, landslides, and long fault-bounded floors. It helps define the immense scale of the canyon system before the terrain opens eastward into the central chasmata.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Ius Chasma is one of the places where Valles Marineris starts to feel less like a single canyon and more like an entire broken world of parallel trenches.

features.name: Melas Chasma
features.description: A deep central section of Valles Marineris famous for dark floor materials and thick layered deposits. Its rocks record a complicated mix of collapse, sedimentation, and possible water-related activity within the canyon system.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Melas Chasma contains some of the deepest exposed terrain on Mars, making it a natural place to read buried chapters of Martian history.

features.name: Argyre Planitia
features.description: A giant impact basin in the southern highlands, smaller than Hellas but still one of the great circular scars on Mars. Its basin floor, surrounding channels, and layered history make it an important marker of ancient impacts and later climate activity.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Argyre is one of the easiest giant basins to recognize on a Mars globe because it appears as a huge round depression ringed by rugged terrain.

features.name: Gusev Crater
features.description: A large crater once considered a strong candidate for an ancient lake basin, later explored by the Spirit rover. Gusev remains important because its floor and nearby Columbia Hills preserve evidence of volcanic resurfacing and hydrothermal alteration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Spirit landed in Gusev expecting lake sediments, then rewrote the story by uncovering a more volcanic and hydrothermal past.

features.name: Chasma Boreale
features.description: A huge canyon slicing into the north polar cap, exposing layered ice and dust that record repeated climate swings. It is one of the most striking named landforms in the martian north and gives the polar region a dramatic sculpted edge.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Chasma Boreale looks like a giant bite taken out of the north polar cap, revealing the layered interior of the ice.

features.name: Australe Scopuli
features.description: A dramatic scarp zone around the south polar layered deposits, where cliffs and troughs mark the edge of the polar ice-rich terrain. It helps give the southern polar region a more legible structure than the cap name alone.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The steep margins of Australe Scopuli help scientists trace how the south polar layered deposits have been built up and carved back over time.
