objects.label: Mercury

sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 VSOP87A full series (Bretagnon and Francou 1988), heliocentric ecliptic J2000, converted to Earth-equatorial J2000
provenance.accuracy: Mercury position was compared with JPL Horizons (DE441) at six dates from 1969 to 2030: at most 30 km (0.11 arcsec) from Horizons. Sample maxima, not a bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Geometric position about the Sun's centre; no light-time or aberration.

objects.description: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with a heavily cratered surface and no moon.

features.name: Caloris Planitia
features.description: One of the largest impact basins in the Solar System, stretching about 1,550 km across. Caloris formed when a massive impact shattered Mercury's crust and was later partly resurfaced by smooth volcanic plains.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Caloris is Latin for 'heat,' reflecting the basin's location near Mercury's hot equatorial region.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The shock from the Caloris impact likely converged on the opposite side of Mercury and helped create the planet's strange chaotic terrain.

features.name: Tolstoj
features.description: An ancient multi-ring impact basin roughly 390 km across, preserving some of Mercury's oldest visible crust. Its worn appearance makes it a key marker for the planet's early bombardment history.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Leo Tolstoy, the Russian novelist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tolstoj is so old that geologists use it to help define one of Mercury's earliest major geologic time periods.

features.name: Rembrandt
features.description: A spectacular 715 km wide impact basin with fractured floor material, smooth plains, and a broad ring structure. It is one of the younger large basins on Mercury and records both impact and volcanic resurfacing.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after the Dutch painter Rembrandt van Rijn.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Rembrandt was one of the standout discoveries of the MESSENGER mission because it had been hidden from Mariner 10's view.

features.name: Beethoven
features.description: A large, old impact basin about 640 km across with subdued rings and widespread smooth plains. It shows how later volcanism and impacts modified Mercury's giant early basins.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Ludwig van Beethoven, the German composer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Beethoven was one of the major named basins already visible in the Mariner 10 era, long before Mercury was globally mapped.

features.name: Kuiper
features.description: A relatively young bright-rayed crater that stands out sharply against Mercury's darker surrounding terrain. Its freshness makes it a useful comparison point for younger impact processes on the planet.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Gerard Kuiper, a pioneering planetary scientist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Kuiper is one of the easiest Mercurian craters to spot in global imagery because its bright rays look so fresh.

features.name: Raphael
features.description: One of Mercury's largest named craters, Raphael is a huge multi-ring impact structure whose broad floor and broken rim preserve the scale of the collisions that shaped the planet's older crust. It belongs with Shakespeare among the giant crater landmarks that make Mercury feel battered on a planetary scale.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Raphael, the Italian Renaissance painter.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Raphael is large enough that, in regional views, it reads less like a single crater and more like a major terrain province cut into Mercury's ancient surface.

features.name: Debussy
features.description: A striking bright-rayed crater in Mercury's southern hemisphere, Debussy stands out because its fresh ejecta streaks slash across much older terrain. It is one of the easiest impact features to pick out in the explorer when scanning east and south of Kuiper.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Claude Debussy, the French composer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Debussy's extensive ray system makes it look geologically young compared with the darker, more muted crater fields around it.

features.name: Hiroshige
features.description: Hiroshige is a broad impact crater northeast of Debussy that reads clearly in regional views because of its size and preserved rim. It helps anchor the dense southern cratered terrain with another obvious named landmark near the Debussy-Kuiper region.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Utagawa Hiroshige, the Japanese artist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Crater naming on Mercury turns regional exploration into a survey of major artists and composers, and Hiroshige is one of the names that stands out once you start using coordinates to hunt features.

features.name: Shakespeare
features.description: A large crater with a broad floor and pronounced rim, named under Mercury's convention of honoring artists, authors, and composers. It is part of the heavily cratered landscape that dominates much of the planet.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after William Shakespeare.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's crater naming theme means the map reads like a global roll call of major artists and writers.

features.name: Matisse
features.description: A well-preserved crater with central peaks and textured ejecta, representing the medium-size impact structures that pepper Mercury's ancient crust. Features like Matisse help compare Mercurian crater morphology with the Moon.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Henri Matisse, the French artist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Mercury and the Moon are both airless worlds, craters like Matisse are useful for direct cross-planet comparison.

features.name: Discovery Rupes
features.description: One of Mercury's giant lobate scarps, a cliff-like thrust fault created as the planet cooled and contracted. These scarps are among the clearest signs that Mercury shrank as its interior lost heat.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after HMS Discovery, continuing Mercury's rupes convention of honoring ships of exploration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's scarps show that the whole planet actually got smaller over time as it cooled.

features.name: Hero Rupes
features.description: A long cliff-like scarp that cuts across older terrain, recording tectonic compression as Mercury's crust adjusted to planetary cooling. Features like Hero Rupes reveal that Mercury remained tectonically active after its heaviest bombardment era.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after HMS Hero, following Mercury's ship-naming rule for rupes features.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some Mercurian scarps are hundreds of kilometers long, making them enormous cliffs on a planet only slightly larger than Earth's Moon.

features.name: Pantheon Fossae
features.description: A striking web of radial troughs near the center of Caloris Basin, often compared to spokes spreading from a wheel hub. The feature likely formed as the basin floor was uplifted, fractured, and modified by volcanism and tectonics.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Pantheon is named after the famous domed temple in Rome.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pantheon Fossae is sometimes nicknamed 'the Spider' because its radial fractures look like legs spreading out across Caloris.

features.name: Northern Smooth Plains
features.description: A vast expanse of relatively smooth terrain interpreted as ancient flood volcanism. These plains indicate Mercury experienced major episodes of lava flooding, not just impact cratering.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The northern smooth plains were one of the strongest pieces of evidence that Mercury had major volcanic resurfacing, not only impact-driven geology.

features.name: Mercury North Pole
features.description: Mercury's north polar region contains permanently shadowed crater floors that never see direct sunlight. Radar and spacecraft data show these cold traps likely preserve water ice despite Mercury's intense proximity to the Sun.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Even on the innermost planet, some crater floors are cold enough to hide water ice for long periods.

features.name: Mercury South Pole
features.description: The south polar region also hosts permanently shadowed craters that are strong candidates for water-ice deposits. These polar cold traps are among Mercury's most surprising discoveries.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's poles are a reminder that temperature on an airless world can depend more on sunlight geometry than distance from the Sun.

provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

knownLimitations: Neptune's picture is a Solar System Scope map (CC BY 4.0) based on NASA imagery; its clouds are a stand-in, not a view of any one day.
The surface drawn is the 1-bar cloud-top level, not a solid surface.
The rings are drawn as flat bands in Planetary Explorer's colours; a ring narrower than the picture can show is drawn wider than it is. Brightness is a look, not a measurement.

families.label: Triton
families.description: By far the largest moon of Neptune, on a retrograde orbit; most likely a captured dwarf planet. It has a Planetary Explorer map.

families.label: Inner moons
families.description: Seven small regular moons close to Neptune on near-circular orbits inside Triton's (Naiad to Proteus, with Hippocamp).

families.label: Sao group
families.description: Three irregular moons on prograde orbits at similar distances, Sao, Laomedeia and S/2002 N 5.

families.label: Neso group
families.description: Three irregular moons on retrograde orbits at similar distances, Psamathe, Neso and S/2021 N 1; Neso has the widest orbit of any moon in the solar system.

families.label: Loners
families.description: Nereid, a large prograde moon on a very elongated orbit, and Halimede, a retrograde irregular moon: in no published group.

features.name: Great Dark Spot
features.description: The Great Dark Spot was a giant anticyclonic storm photographed by Voyager 2 in 1989, comparable in size to Earth. Unlike Jupiter's Great Red Spot, Neptune's dark spots appear and vanish over timescales of just a few years, showing that the planet's atmosphere is much more transient and mobile.

details.label: Observed
details.value: Voyager 2, 1989

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: By the time Hubble looked again in 1994, the original Great Dark Spot had already disappeared.

features.name: Dark Spot Jr.
features.description: After Voyager's Great Dark Spot vanished, Hubble discovered a new generation of dark storms forming at different latitudes. These shifting systems show that Neptune's atmosphere can reorganize rapidly, with vortices migrating and dissipating on surprisingly short timescales.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune's dark vortices have been seen drifting toward the equator, where some appear to break apart and disappear.

features.name: The Scooter
features.description: The Scooter is a bright, fast-moving methane-ice cloud system that raced around Neptune much faster than the Great Dark Spot during the Voyager 2 flyby. It revealed the extreme wind shear in Neptune's atmosphere, where some cloud systems outrun others embedded deeper below.

details.label: Wind context
details.value: Linked to some of the fastest measured winds in the Solar System

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Voyager images showed the Scooter lapping the planet faster than the larger dark storm beside it.

features.name: South Polar Vortex
features.description: Neptune's south pole hosts a warm polar vortex with a compact eye-like structure surrounded by bright methane clouds. Infrared observations show warmer air descending there, making it one of the most distinctive polar weather systems in the outer Solar System.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The south polar vortex has often been compared to a giant hurricane, even though Neptune has no solid surface beneath it.

features.name: Equatorial Methane Haze
features.description: Neptune's equatorial region is wrapped in a bright methane-ice haze where sunlight scatters off high-altitude clouds. This pale band helps distinguish vertical structure in an atmosphere otherwise dominated by deep blue methane absorption.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune's blue colour comes largely from methane absorbing red light, leaving the shorter blue wavelengths to dominate.

features.name: Mid-Latitude Bands
features.description: Subtle bright and dark bands wrap Neptune's mid-latitudes, tracing powerful east-west jet streams. They are fainter than Jupiter's belts but still reveal a deeply organized atmosphere beneath the planet's calmer telescopic appearance.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some of Neptune's jet streams reach supersonic speeds relative to the planet's internal sound speed estimates.

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: The north polar region appears less dramatically structured than the south in many observations, but it still shows seasonal haze, polar circulation, and changes tied to Neptune's long year. Because each season lasts decades, the poles evolve slowly from our perspective.

details.label: Year length
details.value: About 165 Earth years

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: A single Neptunian season lasts more than 40 Earth years.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Neptune's south polar region is marked by bright methane clouds and a warm central vortex, making it the most visually distinctive pole on the planet. It became a major target for infrared telescopes trying to understand how Neptune transports heat from its interior.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune radiates more than twice as much energy as it receives from the Sun, helping power its active weather.

features.name: Triton and the Neptune System
features.description: Neptune's broader system is dominated by Triton, a captured Kuiper Belt object that orbits backward relative to Neptune's rotation. That unusual moon, along with Neptune's faint rings and remote location, makes the planet feel more like the threshold of the Kuiper Belt than just another giant planet.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Triton's retrograde orbit strongly suggests it was captured rather than formed alongside Neptune.

provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: South Polar Nitrogen Cap
features.description: Triton's south polar cap is a bright sheet of frozen nitrogen and methane seen by Voyager 2 during southern summer. Seasonal sunlight can warm the frost just enough to mobilize nitrogen, feeding Triton's thin atmosphere and helping drive the geyser-like plumes that made this moon famous.

details.label: Temperature
details.value: Voyager 2 measured about -235 C near Triton

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright southern cap and streaked polar terrain on the Voyager hemisphere

details.label: Source note
details.value: NASA describes Triton as one of the coldest objects Voyager visited, with nitrogen frost covering much of the surface.

features.name: Hili Plume Field
features.description: Voyager 2 saw dark plume deposits crossing Triton's southern polar terrain, evidence that sunlight can trigger nitrogen geysers through translucent frost. The plumes were only a few active jets in a much broader seasonal system, but they proved Triton was not a dead iceball at the edge of the Solar System.

details.label: Science value
details.value: One of the clearest signs of present-day geologic activity on Triton

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark wind-blown streaks over the southern cap

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Representative plume-field anchor placed on the visible southern streak terrain

features.name: Mahilani Plume Field
features.description: Mahilani marks the second classic plume region associated with Voyager's Triton encounter. Its dark fallout streaks are thought to be carried by Triton's tenuous winds, turning small jets into long surface signatures that reveal both active geology and atmospheric motion.

details.label: Process
details.value: Solar heating through nitrogen frost can pressurize gas below the surface

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dark linear deposits in southern polar terrain

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Representative anchor on the Voyager-mapped plume-streak zone

features.name: Tuonela Planitia
features.description: Tuonela Planitia is an elongated northern plain interpreted as a cryolava lake or resurfaced basin. It cuts across Triton's strange cantaloupe terrain, giving the map a strong contrast between cellular older-looking texture and smoother icy plains that may have flowed or ponded.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: About 400 by 150 km in published descriptions

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Northern smooth/walled plain set among pitted cantaloupe terrain

features.name: Ruach Planitia
features.description: Ruach Planitia is one of Triton's prominent smooth plains, a place where icy material appears to have resurfaced older terrain. Plains like Ruach make Triton look geologically young: impact craters are scarce, and the surface has been repeatedly modified by icy volcanism, collapse, and frost transport.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Smooth northern plain near Tuonela Planitia and the cantaloupe terrain

details.label: Interpretation
details.value: A possible cryovolcanic or volatile-rich resurfacing province

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Educational anchor aligned to the visible northern plains cluster

features.name: Set Catena
features.description: Set Catena is a chain of regularly spaced pits cutting through Triton's northern terrain. Pit chains can form when the crust collapses over voids or fractures, so this feature is a useful stop for reading how Triton's icy shell stretched, broke, and possibly vented volatile-rich material.

details.label: Control coordinate
details.value: About 22 N, 33.5 E

details.label: Typical pit spacing
details.value: Published summaries describe spacing near 20 km

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Linear pit chain in the mapped northern hemisphere

features.name: Bubembe Regio
features.description: Bubembe Regio is part of Triton's named northern terrain province. Its cellular, dimpled texture belongs to the famous 'cantaloupe terrain' seen nowhere else in the Solar System, probably shaped by icy diapirs, collapse, or repeated deformation of a nitrogen-rich crust.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Regio: a broad named region with distinct appearance

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Dimpled northern province west of the main mapped plains cluster

features.name: Monad Regio
features.description: Monad Regio contains some of the most recognizable cantaloupe terrain on Triton. Rounded cells and pitted boundaries make the crust look kneaded rather than cratered, hinting that Triton's interior and volatile cycle have repeatedly renewed its icy surface.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Northern dimpled terrain surrounding Tuonela and Ruach Planitiae

details.label: Science value
details.value: A key terrain for testing how icy shells deform on captured Kuiper Belt objects

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Representative regional anchor on the Voyager global map

features.name: Cipango Planum
features.description: Cipango Planum is a broad, relatively smooth plain in the mapped hemisphere. It helps connect the story of Triton's surface: some areas are heavily textured and cellular, while nearby plains look resurfaced by soft, volatile-rich ice that behaved more like lava than rock.

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Low northern to equatorial smooth terrain near the Set Catena area

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Representative plain anchor placed within the mapped Cipango province

features.name: Leviathan Patera
features.description: Leviathan Patera is one of Triton's named volcanic-looking depressions. Features like this are not basaltic volcanoes; on Triton, eruptions and collapses would involve nitrogen, water ice, ammonia-bearing slurries, or other cryogenic materials in a world colder than any active volcanic body on Earth.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Patera: an irregular crater or volcanic depression

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Northern mapped terrain near pit chains and smooth plains

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Representative anchor for the named cryovolcanic province

features.name: North Polar Seasonal Region
features.description: Triton's north pole was poorly lit for Voyager 2, but it matters because Triton's extreme axial geometry lets each pole take long turns facing the Sun. That seasonal forcing moves nitrogen frost between hemispheres and may change the atmosphere over decades.

details.label: Seasonal context
details.value: Both poles take turns facing the Sun because of Triton's unusual orbit and orientation

details.label: Map cue
details.value: High-latitude reference point, not a sharply imaged named feature

features.name: Retrograde Captured Orbit
features.description: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System with a retrograde orbit: it travels around Neptune opposite the planet's rotation. That dynamical oddity is the strongest clue that Triton began as a Kuiper Belt object and was captured by Neptune rather than forming in place.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 354,800 km from Neptune's center

details.label: Inclination
details.value: About 157 degrees to Neptune's equator, making the orbit retrograde

details.label: Scene note
details.value: Shown as a tilted outer companion path around Neptune

families.label: Charon
families.description: Pluto's big companion, half Pluto's width; the two circle a point between them. It has a Planetary Explorer map.

families.label: The four small moons
families.description: Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra: small irregular moons circling Pluto and Charon together, in near-resonance with Charon's orbit, perhaps made from the debris of the impact that formed Charon.

features.name: Sputnik Planitia
features.description: Sputnik Planitia is the bright western lobe of Pluto's famous heart-shaped region, a vast basin filled with convecting nitrogen ice. The surface is divided into polygonal cells that slowly overturn like a frozen lava lamp, making it one of the most active icy landscapes ever seen in the outer Solar System.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: ~900 × 2,000 km; one of the largest known impact basins in the Solar System

details.label: Depth
details.value: ~3 km below surrounding terrain — likely an ancient impact basin refilled with ice

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The convection cells in Sputnik Planitia may overturn on timescales of hundreds of thousands of years, extremely fast by planetary standards.

features.name: Tombaugh Regio
features.description: Tombaugh Regio is Pluto's iconic bright 'heart', named for Pluto's discoverer Clyde Tombaugh. Spanning roughly 1,600 km across, it is divided into two contrasting lobes: the smooth nitrogen-ice plains of Sputnik Planitia to the west, and a rougher, more mottled eastern lobe of older ices and complex terrain. That hemispheric contrast reveals a world shaped by volatile cycling, where ices migrate, pool, and sublime on geological timescales.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: ~1,600 km across — roughly the distance from New York to Denver

details.label: Western lobe
details.value: Sputnik Planitia — actively convecting nitrogen-ice plains

details.label: Eastern lobe
details.value: Rougher terrain of older, mixed ices with more subdued brightness

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The heart became the defining image of Pluto almost immediately after New Horizons returned its first close-up mosaics in 2015.

features.name: Cthulhu Macula
features.description: Cthulhu Macula is a long dark equatorial region coated in reddish organic compounds called tholins. It preserves some of Pluto's oldest visible surface and contrasts dramatically with the bright volatile plains of Tombaugh Regio, making Pluto a world of stark hemispheric and chemical oppositions.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: ~3,000 km long — stretches more than a quarter of the way around Pluto

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tholins form when sunlight and radiation process simple gases like methane into complex reddish organic residues.

features.name: Elliot Crater
features.description: Elliot Crater is a named impact crater on Pluto's northern encounter hemisphere. Its preserved bowl and rim mark one of the older, more stable terrains outside the active volatile-ice plains of Sputnik Planitia, where impacts remain visible instead of being erased by flowing nitrogen ice.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: ~96 km

details.label: Named for
details.value: James L. Elliot, astronomer whose stellar-occultation work helped reveal atmospheres and ring systems in the outer Solar System

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 12.04°N, 138.86°E; app longitude remap: east - 180.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Craters like Elliot are valuable age markers on Pluto because nearby volatile-ice terrains can renew themselves and erase older impact records.

features.name: Edgeworth Crater
features.description: Edgeworth Crater is a large impact crater on Pluto's encounter hemisphere. Its location away from Sputnik Planitia places it in older terrain where cratering, irradiation, and volatile migration have left a more durable record of Pluto's geological history.

details.label: Named for
details.value: Kenneth Edgeworth, who proposed that small icy bodies could exist beyond Neptune

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 6.86°N, 109.42°E; app longitude remap: east - 180.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Edgeworth's name is tied to the Edgeworth-Kuiper Belt, the distant population of icy worlds that includes Pluto.

features.name: Oort Crater
features.description: Oort Crater is a named impact crater on Pluto, set in terrain that contrasts with the smooth, active deposits around Sputnik Planitia. It represents the cratered record of the Kuiper Belt environment, where impacts have shaped Pluto's surface over billions of years.

details.label: Named for
details.value: Jan Oort, Dutch astronomer associated with the distant comet reservoir known as the Oort Cloud

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 7.86°N, 92.05°E; app longitude remap: east - 180.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pluto's surface preserves clues from both the Kuiper Belt and more distant comet populations studied by astronomers like Oort.

features.name: Lowell Regio
features.description: Lowell Regio is Pluto's bright north polar terrain, a broad cap enriched in methane and ethane ices that tint it a distinctive pale orange. Unlike the nitrogen-rich Sputnik Planitia, Lowell Regio's volatiles are less mobile and accumulate over the long polar seasons of Pluto's 248-year orbit. Named for Percival Lowell, who built the observatory that would eventually yield Pluto's discovery, it is one of the most visually striking regions in the New Horizons full-disc images of Pluto.

details.label: Dominant ices
details.value: Methane (CH₄) and ethane (C₂H₆) — heavier volatiles that resist sublimation near the pole

details.label: Colour
details.value: Pale orange tint from photolytic processing of methane ice into complex organic residues

details.label: Named for
details.value: Percival Lowell (1855–1916), founder of Lowell Observatory, where Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pluto's axial tilt of 119° means its poles experience decades of continuous sunlight and darkness — shaping polar ice deposits unlike anything in the inner Solar System.

features.name: Voyager Terra
features.description: Voyager Terra is a vast, dark northern terrain unit stretching across a large portion of Pluto's northern hemisphere. Its surface is mantled in reddish-brown tholins, giving it a colour similar to Cthulhu Macula at lower latitudes. Voyager Terra is one of Pluto's most ancient surfaces — heavily processed by billions of years of cosmic radiation and volatile cycling — and its rugged, pitted landscape contrasts sharply with the smooth brightness of Lowell Regio and Tombaugh Regio nearby. Named in honour of the twin Voyager spacecraft that revolutionised our understanding of the outer Solar System.

details.label: Surface age
details.value: Among the oldest visible terrain on Pluto, preserving a long record of bombardment and irradiation

details.label: Colour
details.value: Reddish-brown tholins — similar chemistry to Cthulhu Macula but at higher latitudes

details.label: Named for
details.value: NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft, which explored the giant planet systems in the 1970s and 80s

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Although the Voyager spacecraft never reached Pluto, their legacy of outer Solar System exploration made naming this vast dark terrain after them especially fitting.

features.name: Norgay and Hillary Montes
features.description: Towering mountain ranges rise along the margins of Sputnik Planitia, built from bedrock-hard water ice. On Pluto, volatile ices like nitrogen and methane are soft and mobile, so the mountains stand above them like rocky peaks above glaciers on Earth.

details.label: Relief
details.value: Several peaks rise 3 to 5 km above surrounding terrain

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: At Pluto's surface temperature, water ice behaves more like solid rock than like snow.

features.name: Wright Mons
features.description: Wright Mons is one of Pluto's largest and most unusual landforms — a broad mountain in the southern hemisphere roughly 150 km across and 5 km tall, with a wide summit depression several kilometres deep. Its shape is strikingly similar to volcanic shield structures on Earth, and scientists believe it may have been built by repeated eruptions of slushy water-ice from Pluto's interior. If confirmed as a cryovolcano, it would indicate that even a small, distant world in the Kuiper Belt can sustain interior activity long after its formation.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: ~150 km wide, ~5 km tall

details.label: Summit depression
details.value: Several kilometres deep — analogous to the caldera of a volcanic shield

details.label: Location
details.value: Southern hemisphere, southwest of Sputnik Planitia

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Possible cryovolcanoes on Pluto suggest even small distant worlds can remain geologically surprising.

features.name: Bladed Terrain of Tartarus Dorsa
features.description: Tartarus Dorsa is covered in strange knife-edged ridges of methane ice, some hundreds of metres tall. No directly analogous landscape is known elsewhere in the Solar System, making Pluto's bladed terrain one of New Horizons' most alien discoveries.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The blades may form by a process similar to penitentes on Earth, where ice slowly sublimates into towering sharp ridges.

features.name: Charon and the Pluto System
features.description: Pluto and Charon form a binary-like system, with both bodies orbiting a point in space outside Pluto itself. That unusual pairing, along with Pluto's smaller moons and location in the Kuiper Belt, makes the system feel more like a miniature planetary architecture than a lone frozen world.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pluto and Charon are tidally locked to each other, always showing the same face across the gap.

sources: Place names, kinds, descriptions and coordinates: Planetary Explorer's feature lists
Map pictures: USGS Astrogeology and NASA mission mosaics
provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Mordor Macula
features.description: Mordor Macula is Charon's striking reddish-brown northern polar cap — one of the most unexpected discoveries of the 2015 New Horizons flyby. Unlike polar caps elsewhere in the Solar System, Mordor is not composed of ice deposited from within Charon. Instead, it is a vast cap of tholins: complex reddish organic molecules that form when ultraviolet radiation and cosmic rays process methane and nitrogen gas that escapes from Pluto, migrates across space, and freezes out at Charon's pole during its 124-year-long winters.

details.label: Approximate extent
details.value: Covers roughly the top 10–15° of Charon's northern hemisphere

details.label: Colour source
details.value: Tholins — radiation-processed organic molecules originating from Pluto's atmosphere

details.label: Formation mechanism
details.value: Pluto's escaped gases freeze onto Charon's cold winter pole, then irradiation converts the ice into dark, reddish compounds

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Charon's polar night lasts about 62 years — long enough to build up a significant tholins deposit with each cycle.

features.name: Serenity Chasma
features.description: Serenity Chasma is part of Charon's spectacular equatorial canyon system, a series of fractures and troughs that stretches over 1,600 km across the moon's face — comparable to the combined length of all the canyons within the Valles Marineris on Mars. The canyon system, of which Serenity is the most prominent named segment, formed as Charon's interior ocean froze solid early in its history, expanding and cracking the outer crust like a freezing water pipe.

details.label: Total rift system length
details.value: Over 1,600 km

details.label: Depth
details.value: Estimated 5–9 km in places

details.label: Formation
details.value: Crust fracturing as a subsurface ocean froze and expanded during early cooling

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Charon's canyon system is proportionally far more dramatic than Mars's Valles Marineris relative to the body's size.

features.name: Mandjet Chasma
features.description: Mandjet Chasma is one of the great troughs in Charon's global tectonic belt, running along the northern edge of Vulcan Planitia. Its broad, fault-bounded floor records crustal extension as Charon cooled and its interior evolved, making it a key link between the fractured highlands of Oz Terra and the smoother resurfaced plains to the south.

details.label: Approximate length
details.value: ~385 km in the IAU Gazetteer; mapped tectonic interpretations trace the system for at least 450 km

details.label: Relief
details.value: Walls descend roughly 5 to 7 km into the chasma floor in stereoscopic New Horizons topography

details.label: Named for
details.value: The Mandjet, the daytime boat of the Egyptian sun god Ra

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 4.80°N, 294.40°E; app longitude remap: 360 - east.

features.name: Argo Chasma
features.description: Argo Chasma is a large tectonic canyon near Charon's limb in New Horizons views. Its position and alignment show that Charon's extensional fractures were not confined to the central encounter face, but continued around the moon as part of a broader system of crustal stretching.

details.label: Depth
details.value: At least ~5 km deep from New Horizons limb observations

details.label: Named for
details.value: Argo, the ship sailed by Jason and the Argonauts in Greek mythology

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 27.80°N, 80.40°E.

features.name: Caleuche Chasma
features.description: Caleuche Chasma is a high-northern canyon on Charon, cutting through the rugged terrain near Oz Terra and Neverland Regio. Its Y-shaped form and great depth make it one of the most dramatic tectonic scars on the moon, preserving evidence of intense extension in Charon's icy crust.

details.label: Depth
details.value: Reported as roughly 13 km deep, making it one of Charon's deepest known features

details.label: Named for
details.value: El Caleuche, a legendary ghost ship from Chilote mythology in southern Chile

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 72.50°N, 241.80°E; app longitude remap: 360 - east.

features.name: Clarke Montes
features.description: Clarke Montes is a rugged mountain range running along the equatorial zone of Charon's encounter hemisphere, closely associated with the canyon system that divides the moon's two great geological provinces. Individual peaks rise several kilometres above the surrounding terrain, making them the most visually prominent relief features on Charon's face. Their proximity to the canyon suggests they may have been uplifted as the crust fractured — slabs of crust pushed skyward as the rifting system propagated. Named after science fiction author Arthur C. Clarke, whose work helped inspire generations of planetary scientists.

details.label: Location
details.value: Along the equatorial canyon system on the encounter hemisphere

details.label: Peak heights
details.value: Individual summits estimated at 3–5 km above surrounding terrain

details.label: Named for
details.value: Arthur C. Clarke (1917–2008), author of 2001: A Space Odyssey and visionary of space exploration

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The mountains and canyon together divide Charon into two distinct worlds: ancient cratered Oz Terra to the north and smoother, resurfaced Vulcan Planitia to the south.

features.name: Oz Terra
features.description: Oz Terra is the informal name for Charon's rugged, heavily cratered northern terrain, lying just south of the dark Mordor Macula cap. Its densely pitted surface records billions of years of impact bombardment and represents some of the oldest preserved crust on Charon. The high crater density contrasts sharply with the smoother plains of Vulcan Planitia to the south, suggesting dramatically different geological histories for Charon's two hemispheres.

details.label: Character
details.value: Heavily cratered, rugged highland terrain

details.label: Age
details.value: Among the most ancient preserved surfaces on Charon

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The sharp boundary between the old Oz Terra craterlands and the smooth Vulcan Planitia plains suggests a global resurfacing event reset Charon's southern hemisphere long ago.

features.name: Vulcan Planitia
features.description: Vulcan Planitia dominates Charon's encounter hemisphere as a broad, relatively smooth plain marked by gently rolling hills, isolated moats, and scattered small craters. Its smoothness compared to Oz Terra to the north is evidence of ancient cryovolcanic resurfacing — a period when warm slurry of water-ice erupted through the crust and flooded the southern plains, erasing whatever older terrain existed. Named for the Roman god of fire, Vulcan Planitia is Charon's largest recognized geological unit.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: Roughly 800 × 500 km

details.label: Formation
details.value: Cryovolcanic flooding during an early warm period

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Vulcan Planitia is so smooth relative to Oz Terra that scientists believe it was completely resurfaced by liquid water or slush erupting from below after major impacts thinned the crust.

features.name: Kubrick Mons
features.description: Kubrick Mons is an isolated mountain near the southern margin of Mordor Macula, named after filmmaker Stanley Kubrick. It is one of several prominent peaks dotting Charon's surface that appear to have risen isostatically from the crust rather than through volcanic extrusion. Its steep flanks and sharp summit make it a striking landmark where the ancient dark cap meets the rugged Oz Terra highlands.

details.label: Estimated height
details.value: ~3–4 km above surrounding terrain

details.label: Location
details.value: Near the southern margin of Mordor Macula

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Several mountains near Mordor Macula are informally named after famous science fiction directors, forming a crater-and-peak landscape of pop-culture geography.

features.name: Dorothy Crater
features.description: Dorothy Crater is one of Charon's larger named impact craters, located in Oz Terra's rough highlands. Its well-preserved ejecta blanket and central peak structure suggest a relatively young age, though still ancient by Earth standards. Craters in Oz Terra carry Wizard of Oz-inspired names, a naming theme chosen because the region was informally called Oz Terra during mission operations.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: ~230 km (rough estimate from limited-resolution imaging)

details.label: Terrain context
details.value: Oz Terra — Charon's ancient northern highland region

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Craters and features on Charon are named after fictional explorers, adventurers, and the authors and directors who created them.

features.name: Nemo Crater
features.description: Nemo Crater sits near the transition zone between the smooth Vulcan Planitia plains and the rougher terrain to the north, making it a natural laboratory for studying how impact craters interact with two very different surface types. Named after Jules Verne's Captain Nemo, it is part of a cluster of features on Charon informally named after explorers — real and fictional — who ventured into unknown territory.

details.label: Location
details.value: Near the Vulcan Planitia / Oz Terra boundary

details.label: Science value
details.value: Straddles two distinct terrain types, allowing direct comparison of impact morphology across geological units

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Charon's craters are named after legendary explorers — a fitting tribute for a world first seen up close only in 2015.

features.name: Spock Crater
features.description: Spock Crater is a well-defined impact crater set within the smooth plains of Vulcan Planitia. Its crisp rim and relatively shallow depth compared to craters in the older Oz Terra highlands reflect the different properties of the cryovolcanically resurfaced material beneath it. Like many features on Charon, Spock was informally named after a beloved fictional character — Mr. Spock of Star Trek — following the mission team's tradition of naming Charon's craters after legendary space explorers, both real and imagined.

details.label: Location
details.value: Vulcan Planitia — Charon's southern smooth plains

details.label: Named for
details.value: Mr. Spock from Star Trek, created by Gene Roddenberry — a fitting choice for a crater on the plains named after the Roman god Vulcan

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The New Horizons team named Spock Crater in Vulcan Planitia as a deliberate Star Trek homage — Spock, the Vulcan, on a plain named Vulcan.

knownLimitations: Saturn's picture is a Solar System Scope map (CC BY 4.0) based on NASA imagery; its bands are a stand-in, not a view of any one day.
The surface drawn is the 1-bar cloud-top level, not a solid surface.

The rings are drawn as flat bands at the published radii in Planetary Explorer's colours; their brightness is a look, not a measurement. The gaps and thin rings the fact sheet gives no width for are not drawn.
The faint E ring and the F ring are not drawn.

families.label: The seven big moons
families.description: Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan and Iapetus: massive enough to be round. Each has a Planetary Explorer map.

families.label: Small regular moons
families.description: The small moons on regular orbits: the ring shepherds and ring moonlets close to Saturn (Pan to Pallene), the pair Janus and Epimetheus that swap orbits, the Trojan moons of Tethys and Dione, and Hyperion.

families.label: Inuit group
families.description: Irregular moons on prograde orbits, 190 to 300 Saturn radii out, inclined 43 to 51 degrees, taken to be pieces of one or a few parent bodies; the Kiviuq and Siarnaq subgroups.

families.label: Gallic group
families.description: Irregular moons on prograde orbits inclined 34 to 41 degrees, taken to be pieces of one parent body; the largest is Albiorix.

families.label: Norse group
families.description: All retrograde irregular moons, the largest group by far; Phoebe is the biggest. Ashton et al. 2025 split it by inclination into the Phoebe, Mundilfari, Kari and low-inclination subgroups.

features.name: North Polar Hexagon
features.description: One of the most striking geometric weather patterns in the solar system — a persistent hexagonal jet stream surrounding Saturn's north pole. Each side of the hexagon is about 14,500 km long, wider than Earth's diameter.

details.label: Side length
details.value: ~14,500 km (wider than Earth)

details.label: Wind speed
details.value: ~300 km/h along jet stream

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The hexagon has persisted since at least Voyager's visit in 1981 and rotates with Saturn's interior — not its upper atmosphere. The shape is likely maintained by a standing wave in the deep jet stream.

features.name: Great White Spot
features.description: Saturn periodically erupts with enormous white storms — the Great White Spots — that can encircle the entire planet. These giant thunderstorm outbreaks occur roughly every Saturnian year (29.5 Earth years), typically at northern summer.

details.label: Recurrence
details.value: ~Every 29.5 Earth years

details.label: Scale
details.value: Can encircle Saturn's full circumference

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The 2010–2011 Great White Spot was the largest in recorded history, eventually wrapping completely around Saturn. Cassini detected lightning strikes 10,000 times more powerful than Earth's.

features.name: South Polar Vortex
features.description: A permanent hurricane-like vortex at Saturn's south pole with a distinct eye and surrounding eyewall. Unlike Earth hurricanes, it doesn't drift — it stays fixed at the pole. An analogous vortex exists at the north pole, where it sits inside the hexagonal jet stream.

details.label: Eye diameter
details.value: ~8,000 km (~2/3 of Earth's diameter)

details.label: Wind speed
details.value: Up to 550 km/h

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Unlike a tropical hurricane which is driven by warm ocean evaporation, Saturn's polar vortex is a permanent deep-atmosphere feature with no equivalent ocean beneath it.

sources: Place names, kinds, descriptions and coordinates: Planetary Explorer's feature lists

provenance.accuracy: Each place is drawn where it was checked against the map picture by eye, not at a surveyed position; a marker can sit a few degrees from the feature's centre, and a polar entry is a representative anchor, not a feature centre.
provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Herschel Crater
features.description: Herschel is Mimas's defining landmark: a 139-kilometre impact basin cut into a moon only about 394 kilometres wide. Its floor, bright central peak, and towering rim make the small icy moon look uncannily like the Death Star.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 139 km

details.label: Rim height
details.value: About 5 km

details.label: Central peak
details.value: About 6 km high

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Herschel impact was so large that shock waves may have fractured terrain on the opposite side of Mimas.

features.name: Herschel Rim
features.description: The raised rim around Herschel marks where the impact lifted and broke Mimas's icy crust. On the global map, the rim is the crisp circular boundary around the basin, with slumped walls and rugged ejecta fading into older cratered terrain.

details.label: Map position
details.value: Northern rim near 20° N, 111° W

details.label: Feature role
details.value: Boundary of Mimas's largest crater

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Herschel's rim is tall enough that, scaled to Earth, it would be comparable to a mountain range encircling a continent-sized basin.

features.name: Arthur
features.description: Arthur is a 64-kilometre crater on Mimas's southern hemisphere. Its preserved outline sits among dense overlapping impacts, a reminder that Mimas has not erased its surface the way active icy moons can.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 64 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: King Arthur of the Round Table

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mimas crater names are drawn from Arthurian legend, echoing the moon's discovery by William Herschel and its largest crater's Herschel name.

features.name: Merlin
features.description: Merlin is a 37-kilometre crater in the rugged southern mid-latitudes. It lies in terrain where impact scars overlap so tightly that the moon's icy crust reads like a collision record.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 37 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: The magician and adviser from Arthurian legend

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Crater counts on worlds like Mimas help scientists compare how long different icy surfaces have been exposed to impacts.

features.name: Gwynevere
features.description: Gwynevere is a 42-kilometre crater set in the heavily battered hemisphere away from Herschel. It gives visitors a strong comparison point: even outside the giant basin, Mimas is crowded with large, long-lived impact scars.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 42 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Queen Gwynevere from Arthurian legend

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: With no air, rain, or active plate tectonics, crater rims on Mimas can remain visible for immense spans of time.

features.name: Tintagil Catena
features.description: Tintagil Catena is a 130-kilometre chain of depressions in Mimas's southern terrain. It is one of the linear features that hints at crustal stress, possibly linked to the shock of the Herschel-forming impact.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 130 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Tintagil, legendary home of Igraine

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The feature was originally treated as a chasma before its name was updated to Tintagil Catena.

features.name: South Polar Small-Crater Terrain
features.description: Near the south pole, Mimas's crater population changes: many craters are smaller than those across the rest of the moon. NASA notes that this pattern may point to later melting or resurfacing in the polar region.

details.label: Typical crater size
details.value: Often 20 km or less

details.label: Map position
details.value: South polar terrain

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The south polar contrast is one of the clues that Mimas may not be quite as simple and frozen as its cratered face suggests.

features.name: Anti-Herschel Crater Fields
features.description: Much of Mimas away from Herschel is blanketed with closely packed impact craters. This ancient terrain preserves a stark contrast with Enceladus, whose active south pole has erased many old scars.

details.label: Surface character
details.value: Heavily cratered ancient ice

details.label: Scientific puzzle
details.value: Mimas appears frozen despite an orbit that should allow tidal heating

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The contrast between frozen Mimas and active Enceladus is sometimes called the Mimas Test for models of icy moon heating.

features.name: Damascus Sulcus
features.description: Damascus Sulcus is one of the four great tiger stripes cut across Enceladus's south polar terrain. The fracture is part of the warm vent system that sprays water vapor, ice grains, salts, and organic-rich material from the moon's buried ocean into space.

details.label: Role
details.value: Primary south polar vent fissure

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 76.90 deg S, 285.87 deg W

details.label: Map cue
details.value: One of the nearly parallel dark-blue fractures crossing the south pole

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cassini flew through plume material from the tiger stripes and directly sampled grains linked to Enceladus's ocean.

features.name: Baghdad Sulcus
features.description: Baghdad Sulcus is one of Enceladus's most important active fractures. Saturn's gravity flexes the moon during each orbit, stressing the icy shell and helping this long canyon leak heat and ocean-derived particles from below.

details.label: Heat source
details.value: Tidal flexing from Saturn's gravity

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 86.90 deg S, 230.54 deg W

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Near-polar tiger stripe anchor deep in the south polar terrain

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Plume output changes over Enceladus's orbit as the fissures are squeezed and relaxed.

features.name: Cairo Sulcus
features.description: Cairo Sulcus is another of the named tiger stripes that slice through the young south polar cap. Its sharp walls and blue-toned fresh ice mark a place where Enceladus's crust has been pulled open instead of left to collect ancient craters.

details.label: Terrain age
details.value: Geologically young compared with Enceladus's older cratered regions

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 80.37 deg S, 154.48 deg W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The south polar terrain is so geologically young that it lacks the heavy cratering seen across most of Enceladus.

features.name: Alexandria Sulcus
features.description: Alexandria Sulcus completes the set of four prominent tiger stripes named by the IAU. Together with Damascus, Baghdad, and Cairo, it forms the distinctive south polar fracture belt that makes Enceladus one of the most active icy worlds known.

details.label: Feature family
details.value: One of the four major named tiger stripe sulci

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 79.41 deg S, 137.56 deg W

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Parallel south polar fracture near the other tiger stripes

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The four tiger stripes were named for places from The Arabian Nights, matching Enceladus's naming theme.

features.name: South Polar Plume Curtain
features.description: A curtain of icy jets rises from vents along the tiger stripes, feeding Saturn's broad E ring with fresh particles. The plume is the reason Enceladus is such a powerful astrobiology target: it lets spacecraft sample ocean material without drilling through the ice.

details.label: Plume height
details.value: Hundreds of kilometres above the surface

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Enceladus is one of the few worlds where a spacecraft has sampled ocean material without landing.

features.name: South Polar Terrain
features.description: The south polar terrain is Enceladus's active engine room. It is warmer, smoother, and less cratered than the surrounding icy shell, with ridges and fractures arranged around the plume-bearing tiger stripes.

details.label: Science value
details.value: Connects surface fractures, internal heat, and the subsurface ocean

details.label: Map cue
details.value: Bright polar cap surrounding the tiger stripe fracture belt

features.name: Sarandib Planitia
features.description: Sarandib Planitia is a broad, smoother plain that contrasts with Enceladus's older battered terrains. Its relatively clean surface points to resurfacing by tectonics, frost deposition, or warm ice movement long after the moon first formed.

details.label: Surface character
details.value: Smoother and less cratered than ancient terrain

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: On Enceladus, smooth plains likely record episodes when warm ice welled up and spread across the surface before freezing solid again.

features.name: Diyar Planitia
features.description: Diyar Planitia is a bright icy plain marked by fractures and relatively few impact scars. It helps tell the larger Enceladus story: this moon has repeatedly refreshed parts of its shell instead of preserving one uniformly ancient surface.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Enceladus reflects nearly all sunlight that reaches it, making it one of the brightest natural objects in the Solar System.

features.name: Samarkand Sulci
features.description: Samarkand Sulci is a long fracture system that runs far from the south polar geyser zone. It shows that Enceladus's icy shell has been globally stressed, cracked, and renewed, not merely disturbed at the active pole.

details.label: Approximate length
details.value: About 360 km

details.label: IAU coordinate anchor
details.value: 30.00 deg N, 327.50 deg W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Samarkand Sulci spans a huge fraction of a moon only about 504 kilometres across.

features.name: Harran Sulci
features.description: Harran Sulci is a broad region of grooved terrain that bounds Diyar Planitia to the north and east. Voyager images showed it as sinuous mountainous ridges, while Cassini later revealed a more complex ridge belt with scarps and cross-cutting fractures.

details.label: Approximate length
details.value: About 276 km

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 26.70 deg N, 237.60 deg W

details.label: Terrain role
details.value: Forms a tectonic boundary around Diyar Planitia

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Researchers have compared the ridge belt texture to fold belts, a sign that Enceladus's icy crust has been compressed and warped.

features.name: Labtayt Sulci
features.description: Labtayt Sulci is a system of deep fractures seen in detail by Cassini during its February 2005 Enceladus flyby. It cuts across the boundary of the south polar terrain, where stresses in the ice appear to have forced the crust open.

details.label: Approximate size
details.value: About 162 km long, 4 km wide, and 1 km deep

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 28.00 deg S, 284.00 deg W

details.label: Science value
details.value: Shows how the south polar terrain connects to older tectonic structures outside the active tiger stripes

features.name: Bassorah Fossa
features.description: Bassorah Fossa is a long, narrow tectonic depression in Enceladus's northern terrain. It adds another piece to the moon's global stress pattern, showing that faulting and extension are not limited to the active south pole.

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 45.40 deg N, 6.30 deg W

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Fossa: a long, narrow depression or trough

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for Bassorah, a location from The Arabian Nights

features.name: Daryabar Fossa
features.description: Daryabar Fossa is an east-west trending trough first seen by Voyager 2 and later sampled in higher resolution by Cassini. Its relationship with Isbanir Fossa suggests linked faulting, offset troughs, and possible spreading-style deformation.

details.label: Approximate length
details.value: About 201 km

details.label: Approximate shape
details.value: About 400 m deep and 4 km wide

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 9.70 deg N, 359.10 deg W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Daryabar means Seaside in Persian, matching its Arabian Nights naming source.

features.name: Isbanir Fossa
features.description: Isbanir Fossa is a north-south trending scarp that cuts across nearby troughs such as Daryabar Fossa. Topographic studies describe it as a west-dipping scarp, and the offsets around it make it a candidate strike-slip or transform-style fault.

details.label: Approximate length
details.value: About 132 km

details.label: Relief
details.value: About 300 m tall

details.label: Coordinate anchor
details.value: Converted from 12.60 deg N, 354.00 deg W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for the home of Fakir Taj in The Arabian Nights

features.name: Dunyazad
features.description: Dunyazad is a named crater in Enceladus's northern terrains. Craters like this are useful contrast points against the youthful south pole because they preserve the older impact history that active regions have erased.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 30.8 km

details.label: IAU coordinate anchor
details.value: 41.51 deg N, 202.04 deg W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Sister of Shahrazad in The Arabian Nights

features.name: Morgiana
features.description: Morgiana is a smaller crater near Dunyazad in the older northern hemisphere. Its preserved rim helps visitors read Enceladus as a world of contrasts: ancient crater fields in some regions and fresh, active ice at the south pole.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 15.4 km

details.label: IAU coordinate anchor
details.value: 31.75 deg N, 196.17 deg W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: The clever slave girl from Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves

features.name: Ithaca Chasma
features.description: Ithaca Chasma is the great tectonic scar of Tethys: a trough system more than a thousand kilometres long that arcs across much of the icy moon. It may record a time when Tethys's interior froze, expanded, and split the outer shell like brittle rock.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 1,219 km in IAU mapping

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: On a moon only about 1,062 km across, Ithaca Chasma is a truly global-scale fracture.

features.name: Ogygia Chasma
features.description: Ogygia Chasma is a shorter northern fracture that adds a second tectonic note to Tethys's battered surface. Its presence shows that the moon's crust did not simply break once around Ithaca Chasma; smaller fault systems also cut through the old ice.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 120 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Ogygia, the island home of Calypso in the Odyssey

features.name: Odysseus
features.description: Odysseus is one of the largest impact basins on any mid-sized icy moon. Its rim spans nearly two-fifths of Tethys's diameter, yet the basin has a softened, relaxed floor rather than the sharp relief expected from a fresh crater.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 445 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: An impact much larger than the Odysseus event might have shattered Tethys outright.

features.name: Scheria Montes
features.description: Scheria Montes rises inside the Odysseus basin, marking the rugged uplift left by the giant impact. This mountainous patch helps make Odysseus more than a simple circular stain: it preserves the rebound and collapse of Tethys's icy crust.

details.label: Mapped diameter
details.value: About 185 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Scheria, island of the Phaeacians visited by Odysseus

features.name: Penelope
features.description: Penelope is the other major crater in the classic Cassini view of Tethys with Odysseus. Its broad rim and battered floor give a strong comparison point for reading impact ages across the anti-Saturn side of the moon.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Faithful wife of Odysseus

features.name: Melanthius
features.description: Melanthius is a huge southern impact crater set in heavily cratered old terrain. Its subdued outline is a reminder that Tethys's water-ice crust can slowly relax large scars over geologic time.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 250 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tethys is so ice-rich that big impact structures can sag and soften even in the deep cold.

features.name: Antinous
features.description: Antinous anchors another large southern crater field. Together with Melanthius and Telemus, it helps show how saturated the old terrain is: new impacts have repeatedly overlapped older scars.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 138 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Chief of Penelope's suitors in the Odyssey

features.name: Telemachus
features.description: Telemachus is a high-northern crater named for the son of Odysseus. It gives the fact sheet a useful polar-region anchor, away from the better-known Odysseus and Ithaca landmarks.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 92 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tethys's named features draw heavily from people and places in Homer's Odyssey.

features.name: Eurycleia
features.description: Eurycleia sits in the northern cratered terrain, where smaller named craters help visitors read the surface beyond the giant basins. Its compact form contrasts with the broad relaxed floors of Odysseus and Penelope.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 31 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: The faithful nurse of Odysseus

features.name: Polyphemus
features.description: Polyphemus is a mid-sized crater near Tethys's equatorial terrain. Its Odyssey name points back to the moon's naming theme, while its placement helps fill the map between the anti-Saturn crater basins and the tectonic chasmata.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 73 km

details.label: Name origin
details.value: The Cyclops encountered by Odysseus

features.name: E-ring Coated Leading Hemisphere
features.description: The leading side of Tethys is dusted by bright icy particles from Saturn's E ring, which is fed by material erupting from Enceladus. NASA's Cassini color maps show this hemisphere as lighter than the radiation-altered trailing side.

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: Brighter leading hemisphere

details.label: Source
details.value: Cassini global color map, PIA18439

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neighboring Enceladus is literally painting Tethys with fresh icy dust.

features.name: Equatorial Pac-Man Band
features.description: Tethys has a bright equatorial band on its leading hemisphere, first noticed by Voyager and clarified by Cassini. The pattern is linked to high-energy electrons trapped in Saturn's magnetic field changing surface ice on a microscopic scale.

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: Bright equatorial band on the leading side

details.label: Source
details.value: Cassini global color map, PIA18439

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Similar thermal patterns on Tethys and Mimas earned the nickname Pac-Man features.

features.name: Dido
features.description: Dido is one of Dione's largest and most prominent craters, a well-preserved impact basin with a distinct rim and interior structure on the sub-Saturn hemisphere. It is a key reference point for mapping the moon's ancient surface.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 23.97°S, 18.82°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dido is named after the legendary founder and first queen of Carthage — one of many Trojans and Romans lending their names to Dione's craters.

features.name: Romulus
features.description: Romulus is a notable crater on Dione's sub-Saturn hemisphere, paired in name with the nearby Remus — the twin founders of Rome. Both craters sit in ancient terrain that predates Dione's later tectonic activity.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 8.15°S, 26.85°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Romulus and Remus appear as a natural pair on Dione just as they do in Roman mythology — the twin brothers who founded Rome.

features.name: Remus
features.description: Remus sits near its mythological twin Romulus on the sub-Saturn hemisphere, both craters preserving sharp rims that testify to the stability of icy crusts in the outer solar system across billions of years.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 13.58°S, 31.90°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: On Earth, ice is soft and short-lived — but in the deep cold of the Saturn system, Dione's ice is as rigid as rock, keeping crater walls like Remus sharp for billions of years.

features.name: Creusa
features.description: Creusa is a well-defined northern crater named after the wife of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid. Its position in Dione's high northern terrain makes it a useful contrast with the lower-latitude Aeneas and Romulus crater fields.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 49.19°N, 76.32°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Creusa is named after the Trojan princess who vanishes in the fall of Troy — her crater on Dione sits in the same hemisphere as Aeneas, just as she was forever linked to him in myth.

features.name: Aeneas
features.description: Aeneas is a large impact crater with a well-defined rim and central structure, one of the most prominent features on Dione's leading hemisphere. It is a key benchmark for comparing the ages of Dione's bright fractured terrain and its older battered plains.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 25.89°N, 46.27°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Crater counts on Dione show its smooth and fractured regions are geologically young compared to the densely pockmarked terrain where Aeneas sits.

features.name: Evander
features.description: Evander is a large, heavily modified impact basin in Dione's ancient cratered terrain near the anti-Saturn hemisphere. Its broad, degraded form and ejecta blanket record an early period of intense bombardment before any tectonic reshaping of the surface.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 57.00°S, 145.00°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dione is dense enough — about 1.48 g/cm³ — that scientists suspect it once harbored a subsurface ocean beneath its icy shell, despite its quiet appearance today.

features.name: Erulus
features.description: Erulus is a crater sitting close to Evander in Dione's ancient anti-Saturn terrain. Its well-defined walls stand as a record of the intense impact history shared by all of Saturn's inner moons.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 35.00°S, 104.76°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: In Virgil's Aeneid, Erulus was a king with three lives and three sets of arms — an apt namesake for a crater whose walls have endured billions of years of bombardment.

features.name: Amata
features.description: Amata is a named crater on Dione's trailing hemisphere. The name is now assigned to a smaller, well-defined crater rather than the older broad basin identification, making it a useful reminder that planetary names can move as imaging improves.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: ~76 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 5.17°N, 279.81°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Amata is named for the mother of Lavinia, wife of Aeneas; the Gazetteer notes that the name was moved in 2008 to a smaller, better-defined crater.

features.name: Eurotas Chasmata
features.description: Eurotas Chasmata is a broad system of troughs and valleys cut into Dione's icy surface by extensional tectonics. These deep gashes expose layered ice and record a period of intense tectonic upheaval on the trailing hemisphere.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Extensional trough system

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 18.00°N, 270.00°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Chasmata on icy moons like Dione form when the crust is pulled apart from below — the same process that creates rift valleys on Earth, but in water ice instead of rock.

features.name: Padua Chasmata
features.description: Padua Chasmata is part of the bright wispy network on Dione's trailing hemisphere, now understood as a system of ice cliffs and fractures rather than diffuse frost stains. These scarps expose fresh clean ice against darker surroundings, rising hundreds of metres above the fractured plains.

details.label: Terrain type
details.value: Bright tectonic scarps

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 17.70°N, 247.17°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Voyager images made Dione's wisps look like painted streaks, but Cassini revealed they are towering fractured cliffs of ice.

features.name: Palatine Chasmata
features.description: Palatine Chasmata traces one of Dione's major tectonic fault systems across the trailing hemisphere. It records an episode when the icy crust was pulled apart — perhaps driven by internal expansion or the gravitational push and pull of Saturn's tidal forces.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 48.00°S, 316.00°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The brightness of Dione's chasmata comes from exposed fresh ice, which is far more reflective than the older radiation-darkened terrain surrounding it.

features.name: Janiculum Dorsa
features.description: Janiculum Dorsa is a long sinuous ridge running across Dione's leading hemisphere, formed by compressional forces that buckled and folded the icy crust. Ridges like this are rare on Dione and stand in contrast to the extensional fractures that dominate the trailing side.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Compressional ridge

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 24.60°N, 144.10°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: While the trailing hemisphere of Dione was being pulled apart by extension, the leading side experienced compression — Janiculum Dorsa is a physical record of that tectonic imbalance.

features.name: Carthage Fossae
features.description: Carthage Fossae is a system of long, narrow troughs etched into Dione's surface by tectonic extension. These linear depressions cut through older terrain and are part of the broader network of fractures that reshaped the trailing hemisphere.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Linear tectonic trough

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 11.93°N, 336.75°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The fossae of Dione are thought to have formed when internal heating caused the moon's icy shell to expand, splitting the surface in long parallel cracks.

features.name: Fidena Fossae
features.description: Fidena Fossae is a set of elongated troughs cutting through the trailing hemisphere, part of the same tectonic episode that produced Dione's famous wispy terrain. The fossae represent places where the crust fractured cleanly rather than developing the towering scarps seen elsewhere.

details.label: Feature type
details.value: Linear tectonic trough

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 0.66°N, 96.00°W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Fossae and chasmata on Dione formed in the same tectonic event but took different forms — fossae opened as clean troughs while chasmata produced tall, bright ice cliffs.

features.name: Wispy Trailing Terrain
features.description: The trailing hemisphere of Dione is crisscrossed by bright wisps that mark a whole network of tectonic fractures and ice cliffs. This terrain is younger than most of the moon's cratered surface and records a past episode of internal activity that cracked and reshaped the outer crust.

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Visual storytelling anchor for the broad trailing wispy terrain, not an exact IAU Gazetteer feature center.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dione's wispy terrain was one of the Saturn system's biggest visual mysteries until Cassini finally resolved it at high resolution and revealed sheer ice scarps instead of frost.

sources: Place names, kinds, descriptions and coordinates: Planetary Explorer's feature lists
Map pictures: USGS Astrogeology and NASA mission mosaics
