provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Tirawa
features.description: Tirawa marks one of Rhea's great ancient impact scars. Its eroded basin rim and battered surroundings make it a useful landmark for reading how heavily the moon's icy crust was cratered early in Saturn-system history.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: Large basin; USGS center feature lists 0 km because the named point is used as the formal anchor.

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 34.20 N, 151.70 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: NASA identifies Tirawa as the giant basin visible near Rhea's limb in late Cassini views, making it one of the moon's signature landmarks.

features.name: Mamaldi
features.description: Mamaldi is a broad, 480 km impact structure that sprawls across Rhea's cratered terrain. Its size makes it one of the best stops for comparing basin-scale impacts with smaller, sharper craters nearby.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 480 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 14.00 N, 184.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for a Nanai creator goddess connected with the creation of the Asian continent and Sakhalin Island.

features.name: Inktomi
features.description: Inktomi is Rhea's bright young showpiece: a 47 km crater with rays of fresh icy ejecta spread across older terrain. Its crisp rays and strong water-ice signature help scientists study one of the more recent major impacts in Saturn's mid-sized moons.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 47 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 14.10 S, 112.10 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Published age estimates place Inktomi among the youngest large craters in Saturn's regular moon system.

features.name: Powehiwehi
features.description: Powehiwehi is a huge crater on Rhea's darker trailing hemisphere. Its broad form helps show how the trailing side has been altered by magnetospheric particles while still preserving the old impact record.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 271 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 8.20 S, 280.40 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for the first female being in Hawaiian myth, paired with Pouliuli.

features.name: Wakonda
features.description: Wakonda is a large northern crater that gives the explorer a high-latitude reference point away from the equatorial ray systems and trailing-hemisphere scarps.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 123 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 48.60 N, 269.70 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for the Sioux great creator of all things.

features.name: Galunlati Chasmata
features.description: Galunlati Chasmata is one of the long fracture systems cutting across Rhea. These troughs and scarps are part of the wispy-looking terrain that hints at tectonic stresses in an otherwise quiet icy moon.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 740 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 38.00 N, 290.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for the vault above the sky in Cherokee creation stories.

features.name: Avaiki Chasmata
features.description: Avaiki Chasmata traces a long set of grooves and scarps through Rhea's fractured hemisphere. It is a strong companion stop to Galunlati for showing that Rhea's surface is more than a static crater field.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 580 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 25.00 N, 279.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for an underworld in Cook Islands mythology.

features.name: Puchou Catenae
features.description: Puchou Catenae is a long chain of aligned depressions. Catenae can record secondary impacts, structural weaknesses, or disrupted impactor fragments, making them useful clues to local surface history.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 620 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 32.00 N, 87.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for a mountain in Chinese mythology connected with the tilting of Earth's axis.

features.name: Onokoro Catenae
features.description: Onokoro Catenae is a southern chain of pits and small craters that cuts across older terrain. Its aligned form gives Rhea's southern hemisphere a different texture from the broad basins and isolated craters.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 240 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 44.70 S, 328.50 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for the island formed by a drop of water from the sword of Izanagi and Izanami.

features.name: Harahvaiti Fossa
features.description: Harahvaiti Fossa is a southern trough system. It gives the map a compact tectonic stop that contrasts with Rhea's longer chasmata and with the impact-dominated landscapes around Mamaldi.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 190 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 36.00 S, 171.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for a beautiful land created by Ahura Mazda in Persian tradition.

features.name: Parun Fossa
features.description: Parun Fossa is a shorter trough south of the equator. Its placement near other southern features makes it a good marker for following Rhea's fractured terrain across the globe.

details.label: Length
details.value: About 120 km

details.label: Coordinate source
details.value: USGS Gazetteer center: 46.50 S, 152.00 W; app longitude remap: 180 - west.

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Named for a river in Nuristan tradition.

features.name: E-ring-coated Leading Hemisphere
features.description: Rhea's leading hemisphere is relatively bright because it is dusted by icy particles from Saturn's E ring, supplied by neighboring Enceladus. The contrast with the darker trailing side is one of the main color stories in the Cassini global map.

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Broad visual storytelling anchor, not an IAU named feature center.

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: NASA's PIA18438 notes the leading hemisphere is lighter while the trailing hemisphere is darker and altered by Saturn's magnetospheric environment.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Rhea is far enough from Enceladus that the E-ring coating is subtler than on closer moons, but it still helps paint the global color pattern.

features.name: Dark Trailing Hemisphere
features.description: The trailing hemisphere carries darker, more radiation-processed colors than the leading side. This broad terrain stop helps connect Rhea's surface appearance to the plasma and particle environment inside Saturn's magnetosphere.

details.label: Coordinate note
details.value: Broad visual storytelling anchor, not an IAU named feature center.

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: The Cassini color map emphasizes the brightness and color difference between the two hemispheres.

details.label: Why it matters
details.value: Leading-trailing color asymmetry is a shared theme across several Saturnian icy moons, but each moon records it differently.

provenance.notes: Markers hide on the far side of the moon and when the moon is drawn small.

features.name: Kraken Mare
features.description: Titan's largest sea sprawls across the north polar region as a branching body of liquid methane and ethane. Cassini views show a coastline cut by bays, islands, and drowned channels, making Kraken Mare one of the clearest places to compare Titan's methane cycle with Earth's water cycle.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 68.0 N, 310.0 W

details.label: Extent
details.value: About 1,170 km across

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Kraken Mare may contain more liquid hydrocarbons than all known oil and natural gas reserves on Earth combined.

features.name: Ligeia Mare
features.description: Ligeia Mare is Titan's second-largest sea and one of Cassini's best-studied targets. Radar observations showed that this alien sea is mostly liquid methane, with a floor likely coated in organic-rich sediment that rains out of Titan's atmosphere.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 79.7 N, 247.9 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 500 km

details.label: Composition
details.value: Predominantly liquid methane, with dissolved nitrogen and other organics

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cassini radar detected echoes from the seafloor, turning Ligeia Mare into the first extraterrestrial sea sounded from orbit.

features.name: Punga Mare
features.description: Punga Mare sits close to Titan's north pole between the larger polar seas and a scatter of smaller lakes. Its compact shape helps show how Titan's polar basins collect methane and ethane into a connected landscape of seas, shorelines, and bright highlands.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 85.1 N, 339.7 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 380 km

details.label: Mission View
details.value: Cassini's final Titan mosaic showed Punga Mare near Ligeia Mare and Kraken Mare in the north polar lake district.

features.name: Ontario Lacus
features.description: Ontario Lacus is Titan's major southern lake, a dark, smooth basin near the south pole. Cassini used it as a key comparison point for understanding why Titan's large liquid reservoirs are concentrated in the north while the south holds only one major lake.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 72.0 S, 183.0 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 235 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Ontario Lacus was one of the first Titan lakes studied closely enough to compare its shoreline and liquid behavior with terrestrial lakes.

features.name: Belet
features.description: Belet is a broad dark equatorial region associated with Titan's immense dune fields. The long, wind-aligned ridges are likely built from organic sand grains produced in the hazy atmosphere and then carried across the surface by seasonal winds.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 5.0 S, 255.0 W

details.label: Texture Cue
details.value: Dark equatorial terrain with repeated linear dune textures

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Titan's dunes are thought to be made from hydrocarbon grains produced high in the atmosphere and dropped slowly to the ground.

features.name: Shangri-La
features.description: Shangri-La is a broad dark terrain crossed by dune-rich equatorial plains and brighter icy islands. The Huygens probe landed on the western side of this region, linking the global map to the only surface images ever taken from Titan.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 10.0 S, 165.0 W

details.label: Mission Link
details.value: Huygens landed west of Shangri-La on January 14, 2005

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The pebbles imaged by Huygens looked river-worn, suggesting methane rains and runoff had rounded them long before the landing.

features.name: Huygens Landing Site
features.description: Huygens descended through Titan's orange haze for more than two hours before touching down on a dark floodplain of icy cobbles and sand. Its images connected orbital hints of channels and shore-like terrain with direct ground truth from the outer solar system.

details.label: Landing Date
details.value: January 14, 2005

details.label: Approximate Coordinates
details.value: About 10.6 S, 192.3 W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Huygens remains the only spacecraft to land on a world in the outer solar system.

features.name: Xanadu
features.description: Xanadu is a vast bright region roughly the size of a continent, standing out against Titan's darker equatorial dune belts. Cassini replaced earlier lower-quality coverage of Xanadu with sharper imaging in the June 2015 global map, making it one of the best visual anchors on Titan's surface.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 15.0 S, 100.0 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 3,400 km

details.label: Texture Cue
details.value: Large bright region contrasting with the darker equatorial terrain

features.name: Menrva
features.description: Menrva is Titan's largest confirmed impact crater, a broad multi-ring basin visible through the moon's haze and surface deposits. It matters because Titan's atmosphere, dunes, and methane weather quickly soften or bury many impact scars.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 20.1 N, 87.2 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 392 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Titan's atmosphere burns up many incoming objects, so only the largest impacts tend to survive as obvious craters.

features.name: Sinlap
features.description: Sinlap is a comparatively crisp impact crater with a dark floor and brighter rim. Its relatively fresh appearance helps scientists judge how fast Titan's winds, haze fallout, and methane-driven erosion can disguise craters.

details.label: Source Coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 11.3 N, 16.0 W

details.label: Diameter
details.value: Roughly 80 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Sinlap is one of the few Titan craters where Cassini could clearly resolve both the rim and ejecta patterns through the thick haze.

features.name: North Polar Lakes
features.description: Titan's north polar terrain is crowded with filled and empty lake basins carved into icy crust. Cassini found that the north holds the moon's great seas plus many smaller lakes, turning this region into the centerpiece of Titan's active methane climate.

details.label: Source Note
details.value: Broad storytelling anchor for the north polar lake district rather than one IAU feature center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some Titan lake basins have steep-sided rims and flat floors, making them look more like sinkholes than ordinary impact craters.

features.name: Cassini Regio
features.description: Cassini Regio is the immense dark terrain wrapped around Iapetus's leading hemisphere, the side that plows forward through Saturn's outer system. Its dusty surface absorbs more sunlight than the bright icy terrain, warms up, and helps drive ice away, reinforcing the moon's famous two-tone contrast.

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 28.1 S, 92.6 W

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: Large dark field centered on the leading hemisphere

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Iapetus was one of the earliest moons where astronomers noticed the same object seemed to brighten and darken dramatically over its orbit.

features.name: Roncevaux Terra
features.description: Roncevaux Terra is a bright northern expanse where water ice still dominates the surface. It helps frame the bright side of Iapetus against the dark leading hemisphere, making the moon look almost as if two different worlds were joined together.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 1,284 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 37.0 N, 239.5 W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The bright trailing side can reflect several times more sunlight than the dark leading side, even though both belong to the same moon.

features.name: Saragossa Terra
features.description: Saragossa Terra spreads across the southern bright terrain as icy highlands broken by very large impact scars. It is the cleaner, frostier counterpart to Cassini Regio and a strong reminder that Iapetus' color pattern is global, not just a small surface stain.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 2,300 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 45.0 S, 180.0 W

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Once the dark side of Iapetus warms enough, it loses bright ice faster, making the moon's colour contrast self-amplifying over time.

features.name: Equatorial Ridge
features.description: Iapetus' equatorial ridge is a chain of mountains and raised terrain that follows the equator across much of the moon, giving Iapetus its distinctive walnut-like outline. Some sections rise dramatically above the surrounding plains, and the ridge remains one of the most unusual structures found on a mid-sized icy moon.

details.label: Texture cue
details.value: Thin equatorial highland chain crossing the dark terrain and named montes segments

details.label: Source note
details.value: Representative educational anchor; named ridge segments are listed separately

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: One idea is that the ridge formed from material that once orbited Iapetus and later collapsed onto the equator.

features.name: Carcassone Montes
features.description: Carcassone Montes is one of the named mountain-chain segments along Iapetus' equatorial ridge. It marks a long stretch of the ridge where the surface rises into a narrow, world-spanning spine instead of spreading into ordinary cratered plains.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 740 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 0.0 N, 216.7 W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Town in southern France sacked by Roland

features.name: Toledo Montes
features.description: Toledo Montes is a broader named section of Iapetus' equatorial ridge. Its placement helps visitors follow the ridge across the globe and see how the raised belt ties together bright and dark terrains.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 1,100 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 0.0 N, 136.0 W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: Spanish town known for blacksmiths' work in the Song of Roland naming theme

features.name: Turgis
features.description: Turgis is one of Iapetus' largest named impact craters, a huge circular scar on the darkened leading side. Its scale makes it a useful anchor for comparing basin-sized impacts against the equatorial ridge and the albedo boundary.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 580 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 16.9 N, 28.4 W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: A Saracen baron, count of Tortelosa, killed by Oliver

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Basins like Turgis help reveal whether Iapetus's crust behaved rigidly like rock or slowly relaxed like warm ice after giant impacts.

features.name: Abisme
features.description: Abisme is a vast northern crater superposed on the dark hemisphere. Its bright and dark materials sit near the heart of Cassini Regio, making it a strong control point for both crater storytelling and texture alignment.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: About 768 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 37.53 N, 92.92 W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: A Saracen lord killed by Archbishop Turpin

features.name: Engelier
features.description: Engelier is a giant southern impact crater set in the brighter terrain of Iapetus. Its immense size and pale surroundings make it a key southern control feature on the Cassini color map.

details.label: Diameter
details.value: 504 km

details.label: Source coordinates
details.value: USGS/IAU center: 40.5 S, 264.7 W

details.label: Texture calibration
details.value: Visual center on the shipped texture: about 42.4 S, 82 W

details.label: Name origin
details.value: One of the Twelve Peers, the Gascon of Bordeaux

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Crater rims crossing the colour boundary on Iapetus can appear half dark and half bright depending on which hemisphere they face.

features.name: Falsaron
features.description: Falsaron is a broad crater in the northern dark terrain, close enough to Abisme to help show how heavily battered Cassini Regio really is. It gives the crater layer another large landmark on the leading hemisphere.

features.name: Gerin
features.description: Gerin is a large southern crater near Engelier in Iapetus' bright terrain. Together, the two craters make the southern hemisphere feel less empty and help compare overlapping impact scales on the icy crust.

details.label: Diameter

features.name: Cassini Boundary Zone
features.description: The transition between dark Cassini Regio and the bright trailing terrain is surprisingly abrupt in places, creating one of the sharpest large-scale color boundaries on any planetary body. It records the interplay between dust deposition, sunlight absorption, and thermal ice migration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The leading hemisphere likely started dark because it sweeps up dust while moving forward through space, like a bug hitting the windshield of a car.

objects.label: Uranus

sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 VSOP87A full series (Bretagnon and Francou 1988), heliocentric ecliptic J2000, converted to Earth-equatorial J2000
provenance.accuracy: Uranus position was compared with JPL Horizons (DE441) at six dates from 1969 to 2030: at most 19,070 km (1.36 arcsec) from Horizons. Sample maxima, not a bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Geometric position about the Sun's centre; no light-time or aberration.

knownLimitations: Uranus's picture is a Solar System Scope map (CC BY 4.0) based on NASA imagery; the planet is nearly featureless in visible light.
The surface drawn is the 1-bar cloud-top level, not a solid surface.

The rings are drawn as flat bands in Planetary Explorer's colours; the nine narrow inner rings are grouped as the donor draws them, and a ring narrower than the picture can show is drawn wider than it is. Brightness is a look, not a measurement.
None of Uranus's moons has a map picture here: all 28 are shown as dots in family colours.

families.label: The five big moons
families.description: Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon: the round moons, found 1787 to 1948.

families.label: Inner moons
families.description: Thirteen small dark moons inside Miranda's orbit, among Uranus's rings (ring shepherds Cordelia and Ophelia, the Portia and Belinda groups, Puck, and Mab, the source of the mu ring).

families.label: Caliban group
families.description: Irregular moons on retrograde orbits with similar distances and inclinations (Caliban, Stephano and S/2023 U 1).

families.label: Other retrograde irregular moons
families.description: Six irregular moons on retrograde orbits that fit no group: Sycorax, Prospero, Setebos, Trinculo, Francisco and Ferdinand.

families.label: Loners
families.description: Margaret, the only known irregular moon of Uranus on a prograde orbit; in no group.

features.name: North Polar Hood
features.description: Uranus's north polar region is capped by a bright methane haze known as the north polar hood. It becomes especially prominent as the pole tilts toward the Sun, making seasonal lighting one of the main reasons Uranus's atmosphere can look dramatically different over decades.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Uranus is tipped on its side, one pole can spend roughly 42 years in continuous sunlight.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: The south polar region once appeared brighter during the Voyager 2 flyby, when Uranus was near southern summer. Long-term monitoring has shown the poles trading prominence as the seasons slowly shift across the planet's 84-year orbit.

details.label: Year length
details.value: 84 Earth years

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Uranus's seasons are so long that no spacecraft has yet seen it under a full range of seasonal conditions.

features.name: Equatorial Band
features.description: A faint bright band wraps Uranus near the equator, produced by subtle changes in methane haze and cloud opacity. It is much more understated than the belts of Jupiter or Saturn, but it reveals that Uranus still has organized atmospheric circulation.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: For decades Uranus looked almost featureless in small telescopes, but modern imaging has revealed faint bands and cloud structure across the disk.

features.name: Mid-Latitude Banding
features.description: Low-contrast bands and zonal flows stripe Uranus's mid-latitudes, though they are muted by the planet's thick methane haze. These belts become more visible in infrared observations, where cloud tops and deeper layers separate more clearly.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Infrared imaging often shows Uranus as a much more structured world than it appears in visible light.

features.name: Bright Northern Storm
features.description: In recent decades astronomers have tracked bright methane-ice storms erupting in Uranus's northern hemisphere, proving that the planet's atmosphere can become unexpectedly active. These outbreaks rise above the surrounding haze and can persist for months.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Large Uranian storms have appeared often enough in the 21st century to surprise scientists who once expected the planet to remain almost inert.

features.name: The Berg
features.description: The Berg was a long-lived cloud feature observed drifting through Uranus's southern mid-latitudes before changing latitude and fading. Its evolution showed that even Uranus's subdued weather can reorganize over time in ways that are dynamically rich rather than static.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Berg was one of the first Uranian storm systems to be tracked over many years with Hubble and large ground-based telescopes.

features.name: Uranian Ring System
features.description: Uranus is surrounded by a set of narrow, dark rings made mostly of radiation-processed water ice mixed with darker material. They are far less luminous than Saturn's broad icy rings, but they form one of the planet's most important structural features and reinforce its distinct sideways geometry.

details.label: Discovery
details.value: Stellar occultation observations, 1977

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Uranus's rings were discovered when they briefly dimmed a star before the planet itself passed in front of it.

features.name: Axial Tilt and Sideways Seasons
features.description: Uranus rotates with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees, essentially rolling around the Sun on its side. That extreme geometry drives the most unusual seasonal cycle in the Solar System, with poles taking turns pointing almost directly at the Sun for decades at a time.

details.label: Tilt
details.value: Approximately 98 degrees

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Around solstice, one Uranian pole experiences continuous daylight while the other sits in decades of darkness.

features.name: Rings and Moon System
features.description: Uranus is orbited by a set of dark narrow rings and a family of icy moons, but the whole system is tipped over with the planet itself. That shared sideways geometry makes Uranus feel architecturally distinct from every other major planet pack in the explorer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: When Uranus's ring plane points edge-on toward Earth, the rings can become extraordinarily difficult to detect.

objects.label: Venus

sources: @lizard-isana/orb 3.1.1 VSOP87A full series (Bretagnon and Francou 1988), heliocentric ecliptic J2000, converted to Earth-equatorial J2000
provenance.accuracy: Venus position was compared with JPL Horizons (DE441) at six dates from 1969 to 2030: at most 50 km (0.10 arcsec) from Horizons. Sample maxima, not a bound for every date.
provenance.notes: Geometric position about the Sun's centre; no light-time or aberration.

objects.description: The hottest planet, wrapped in thick cloud, with no moon.

features.name: Ishtar Terra
features.description: A major highland continent in Venus' northern hemisphere, often compared in scale to Australia. Ishtar Terra gathers some of the planet's most dramatic relief, including Maxwell Montes and Lakshmi Planum.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Ishtar, a Mesopotamian goddess associated with love and war.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Ishtar Terra is one of the strongest examples that Venus is not just smooth plains but also has continent-like elevated regions.

features.name: Aphrodite Terra
features.description: The largest highland region on Venus, stretching for thousands of kilometers near the equator. It contains rifts, tessera terrain, and volcanic provinces that make it one of the planet's most geologically varied landscapes.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Aphrodite Terra is so vast that it behaves more like a continent than a single landmark.

features.name: Maxwell Montes
features.description: The highest mountain range on Venus, rising roughly 11 km above the surrounding terrain. Radar-bright material near its peaks may reflect unusual minerals formed under the planet's extreme conditions.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Unusually for Venus, it is named after James Clerk Maxwell rather than a female figure because the name predates the later naming convention.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Maxwell Montes is one of the rare Venus features whose summit regions may host chemistry unlike the lowlands because of the change in temperature and pressure with altitude.

features.name: Maat Mons
features.description: One of Venus' largest shield volcanoes, with broad flanks and signs of extensive lava flows. Recent scientific analysis has made Maat Mons one of the headline candidates for geologically recent volcanic activity on Venus.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Maat, the Egyptian goddess of truth and cosmic order.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Maat Mons is one of the most talked-about Venus volcanoes because orbital radar comparisons may hint at very recent activity.

features.name: Sapas Mons
features.description: A large volcanic edifice associated with extensive lava flows and dome-like structures. It helps show that Venusian volcanism produced broad, complex surface resurfacing rather than only isolated cones.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after a Phoenician goddess.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Venusian radar maps make volcanoes like Sapas Mons look almost sculpted in metal because the surface is seen through radar, not visible-light photography.

features.name: Artemis Corona
features.description: A gigantic oval corona structure about 2,000 km across, marked by concentric fractures and surrounding tectonic deformation. Coronae are among Venus' signature landforms and may record mantle upwelling and crustal collapse.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Artemis, the Greek goddess associated with wild nature and the hunt.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Artemis Corona is so large that it behaves less like a crater and more like a whole tectonic province.

features.name: Heng-O Corona
features.description: A large fractured corona whose broken rings and surrounding deformation show the classic Venusian pattern of mantle upwelling followed by crustal collapse. It helps widen the corona story beyond Artemis by showing that these circular tectonic systems occur across very different parts of the planet.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Heng-O, a Chinese moon goddess.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Coronae are one of the landforms most strongly associated with Venus because no other rocky planet shows them in such abundance and variety.

features.name: Quetzalpetlatl Corona
features.description: This corona is notable for its concentric fractures, associated volcanic flows, and broad regional deformation. It is one of the best examples of how coronae can blend tectonic and volcanic processes into a single signature Venus landform.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Quetzalpetlatl, an Aztec creator goddess.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Features like Quetzalpetlatl Corona make Venus feel alien in a way the Moon and Mercury do not, because they combine ring-like structures with evidence of internal upwelling instead of simple impact scars.

features.name: Alpha Regio
features.description: A classic tessera terrain region where highly deformed ridges and troughs intersect in multiple directions. Tesserae are some of the oldest and most geologically complex surfaces on Venus.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tessera terrain is often described as Venus' most complicated surface texture, with ridge patterns crossing like woven fabric.

features.name: Ovda Regio
features.description: A vast highland and tessera region within Aphrodite Terra, preserving some of Venus' most intricate deformation patterns. It is central to debates about how Venusian crust formed and evolved.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Ovda Regio is often discussed as a possible key to understanding whether parts of Venus once behaved more like mobile crust than the planet does today.

features.name: Mead
features.description: The largest confirmed impact crater on Venus, more than 270 km across. Its ring structure and preserved ejecta provide important clues about how impacts behave in Venus' dense atmosphere.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after anthropologist Margaret Mead.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Venus has such a thick atmosphere, only larger incoming objects tend to survive to make craters like Mead.

features.name: Isabella
features.description: One of the largest impact craters on Venus, Isabella preserves a prominent ring structure and a broad dark floor that stands out in radar imagery. It helps show that while Venus has relatively few craters, the largest ones become major regional landmarks.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Isabella d'Este, an Italian Renaissance patron of the arts.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: On Venus, big craters like Isabella are especially valuable because the dense atmosphere filters out many smaller impactors before they ever reach the surface.

features.name: Saskia
features.description: A large, well-preserved crater whose bright rim and organized ejecta make it one of the clearer impact landmarks outside the Mead-Cleopatra pair. Saskia strengthens the feeling that Venusian impact sites are rare but visually distinctive when they do occur.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Saskia van Uylenburgh, associated with Dutch Golden Age portraiture.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Venusian craters are relatively sparse, a feature like Saskia can anchor a whole region during visual exploration far more strongly than a similar-sized crater might on Mercury or the Moon.

features.name: Cleopatra
features.description: A radar-bright impact crater perched high within Maxwell Montes. Its unusual setting and outflow-like deposits made it one of the most debated Venus features during the Magellan era.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Cleopatra, queen of ancient Egypt.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cleopatra is famous partly because scientists once argued over whether it was really an impact crater or some exotic volcanic structure.

features.name: Gula Mons
features.description: A major shield volcano with expansive lava flows and a broad summit region, Gula Mons is one of the clearest volcanic landmarks outside the Maat-Sapas area. It helps show that Venusian volcanism is distributed across multiple provinces rather than concentrated in only one cluster.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Gula, a Mesopotamian goddess associated with healing.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Venusian shield volcanoes can be enormous, but because they are mapped by radar they often look smoother and more fluid than comparable volcanoes on Earth.

features.name: Theia Mons
features.description: A large volcanic rise with associated flow fields, Theia Mons helps broaden the explorer's view of Venusian volcanism beyond the best-known equatorial giants. It reinforces the idea that Venus has multiple major volcanic centers spread across the globe.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Theia, a Greek Titan associated with shining light.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Adding volcanoes like Theia Mons makes Venus feel less like a single-feature planet and more like a world shaped by repeated resurfacing in many regions.

features.name: Venera 7 Landing Site
features.description: The site where Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to transmit data from the surface of another planet in 1970. It survived only briefly, but proved that Venus' brutal surface conditions could be directly sampled.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Venera 7 was the first successful soft landing on another planet, even though Venus gave it only a short time to talk back.

features.name: Venera 9 Landing Site
features.description: Venera 9 returned the first image ever taken from the surface of another planet in 1975. Its rocky panorama gave humanity the first direct look at Venus from ground level.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Venera 9's blocky horizon is one of the foundational images in planetary exploration history.

features.name: Venera 13 Landing Site
features.description: Venera 13 returned some of the most famous Venus surface images and measurements in 1982, including color imagery and the sound of equipment operating in the extreme environment. It remains one of the richest direct datasets from Venus' surface.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Venera 13 survived long enough to send back color views and compositional measurements from one of the harshest environments ever reached by a spacecraft.
